docs.title: AutoGen Production Integration
docs.description: Apply OAIES controls when Microsoft AutoGen is selected for multi-agent messaging and teams.
docs.text: AutoGen Production Integration Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Apply OAIES controls when Microsoft AutoGen is selected for multi-agent messaging and teams. Why Conversation and team abstractions simplify coordination but can hide loops, authority boundaries, and correlated-agent failure. How Pin the supported AutoGen release and use typed messages, explicit team membership, bounded termination conditions, isolated tool executors, and an external durable state/audit layer. Authenticate each runtime identity; authorize every tool call against original intent. Persist message digests and artifact provenance, not hidden reasoning. Validate saved-state compatibility before resume. Tradeoffs Flexible conversational routing supports experimentation but is harder to reason about than a fixed workflow graph. Prefer explicit deterministic routing for regulated or irreversible work. Anti-patterns - Letting model text select or extend privileges. - Relying on “consensus” among same-model agents. - Using message count alone as a success condition. Enterprise Considerations Place model clients, tools, and remote runtimes behind tenant-aware gateways. Track framework/model versions in every trace and maintain an exit path through a framework-neutral message/state schema. Checklist - [ ] Typed messages and authenticated runtime identities are enforced. - [ ] Termination covers deadline, budget, no-progress, and cancellation. - [ ] Tool execution is isolated and independently authorized. - [ ] State save/load and upgrade compatibility are tested. References - AutoGen AgentChat documentation - AutoGen termination documentation Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production integration standard.

docs.title: CrewAI Production Integration
docs.description: Apply OAIES controls when CrewAI crews or flows are selected as the orchestration layer.
docs.text: CrewAI Production Integration Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Apply OAIES controls when CrewAI crews or flows are selected as the orchestration layer. Why Role and delegation abstractions are application structure, not security boundaries. Production safety still requires external identity, policy, state, provenance, and budget enforcement. How Use Flows for explicit state and event routing; define Pydantic state schemas and deterministic completion conditions. Disable unconstrained delegation, wrap tools with policy checks and idempotency, and persist checkpoints in a tenant-scoped durable store. Attach authenticated identity, task, delegation, budget, and provenance metadata to every event and output. Tradeoffs Crews provide rapid role composition but increase emergent routing. Prefer a Flow with explicit transitions whenever correctness or auditability is more important than open-ended collaboration. Anti-patterns - Treating role names or backstories as access controls. - Enabling delegation without depth, audience, and budget attenuation. - Depending on framework memory as the system of record. Enterprise Considerations Review telemetry and hosted-service data paths before enabling them. Pin dependencies, scan tool plugins, and keep framework-neutral state and audit exports. Checklist - [ ] Flow state schema and terminal outcomes are explicit. - [ ] Delegation and tools are externally authorized and bounded. - [ ] Persistence is tenant-scoped, encrypted, and recoverable. - [ ] Telemetry, data residency, and dependency risks are approved. References - CrewAI Flows documentation - CrewAI production architecture documentation Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production integration standard.

docs.title: LangGraph Production Integration
docs.description: Apply OAIES controls when LangGraph is selected as the workflow runtime.
docs.text: LangGraph Production Integration Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Apply OAIES controls when LangGraph is selected as the workflow runtime. Why Graph orchestration and checkpoint APIs reduce implementation effort, but do not supply workload identity, authorization, non-repudiation, or business-safe recovery. How Define typed state and explicit nodes/edges; keep authorization outside prompts. Use a durable production checkpointer, stable thread/task IDs, idempotent tools, bounded recursion, interrupts for approvals, and deterministic validators before commits. Encrypt and tenant-scope persisted state, and emit provenance, budget, policy, and checkpoint identifiers to the audit pipeline. Tradeoffs Framework persistence accelerates recovery but couples stored state to graph and library versions. Pin versions and test checkpoint migration before deployment. Anti-patterns - Using in-memory checkpointing in production. - Resuming a checkpoint without re-authorizing credentials and pending actions. - Treating recursionlimit as the only budget or loop control. Enterprise Considerations Wrap framework APIs behind an owned adapter, inventory transitive dependencies, and verify data residency and deletion behavior for the selected checkpoint store. Checklist - [ ] Typed state, migrations, and durable checkpointer are tested. - [ ] Identity, policy, provenance, and budgets remain platform controls. - [ ] Interrupt, cancellation, duplicate delivery, and resume tests pass. - [ ] Graph/library upgrades replay representative checkpoints. References - LangGraph persistence documentation - LangGraph durable execution documentation Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production integration standard.

docs.title: Level 5: Multi-Agent Systems
docs.description: Define the production control plane for systems in which independently executing agents delegate, communicate, and mutate durable state.
docs.text: Level 5: Multi-Agent Systems Version: 2.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Prerequisite: reliable, evaluated single-agent operation Purpose Define the production control plane for systems in which independently executing agents delegate, communicate, and mutate durable state. Why Multiple agents add trust boundaries, failure modes, latency, and cost. Use them only when an evaluated topology outperforms the strongest single-agent baseline on a representative workload. How 1. Establish identity, capability, budget, deadline, and termination policy before dispatch. 2. Use signed, replay-resistant message envelopes and validate provenance at every hop. 3. Commit outputs through versioned checkpoints; never let conversational context be authoritative state. 4. Isolate worker credentials and validate artifacts before privilege is propagated. 5. Compare quality, safety, latency, and cost against a single-agent control before release. Standards Corpus - Architecture and benefit proof - Identity and authenticated delegation - Message provenance and non-repudiation - Durable state and checkpoints - Threat controls - Cost, budgets, and termination - LangGraph integration - AutoGen integration - CrewAI integration Tradeoffs Multi-agent execution can improve parallelism and context isolation, but increases coordination overhead, attack surface, nondeterminism, and observability burden. Central orchestration is the default because ownership and termination remain explicit; peer-to-peer autonomy requires a documented exception. Anti-patterns - Agent count as architecture: roles without measured independent value add cost without capability. - Bearer authority propagation: forwarding a caller token makes every downstream agent a confused-deputy target. - Chat as state: free-form transcripts cannot provide atomicity, conflict detection, or recoverable checkpoints. - Unlimited debate: peer critique without budgets or convergence tests creates loops and collusion risk. Enterprise Considerations Map every agent and service identity to an accountable owner. Retain tamper-evident decision and delegation records according to legal policy, segregate tenants cryptographically and logically, and require human approval for irreversible or regulated actions. Checklist - [ ] Multi-agent benefit is statistically and operationally demonstrated against the single-agent baseline. - [ ] Every delegation is authenticated, audience-bound, least-privilege, and expires. - [ ] Messages are signed, replay-protected, correlated, and retained in a tamper-evident log. - [ ] Durable state supports optimistic concurrency, idempotency, checkpoints, and tested recovery. - [ ] Loop, collusion, confused-deputy, and privilege-propagation tests pass. - [ ] Per-agent and workflow budgets, deadlines, cancellation, and terminal states are enforced. - [ ] Human escalation and emergency revocation are tested end to end. References - NIST AI RMF 1.0 - NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture - RFC 9421, HTTP Message Signatures - OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 Changelog - 2.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Replaced introductory guidance with production identity, provenance, state, threat, budget, and benefit gates.

docs.title: Architecture and Multi-Agent Benefit Standard
docs.description: Prevent unjustified agent decomposition and define evidence required to claim a multi-agent benefit.
docs.text: Architecture and Multi-Agent Benefit Standard Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Prevent unjustified agent decomposition and define evidence required to claim a multi-agent benefit. Why Additional agents are not an intrinsic capability improvement. Coordination can reduce quality while increasing tokens, latency, and failure probability. How 1. Build the strongest single-agent baseline with identical models, tools, data, and total budget. 2. Pre-register representative tasks, success rubrics, safety failures, and operational limits. 3. Choose a topology only for a demonstrated boundary: independent parallel work, privilege isolation, or specialist context. 4. Run paired trials with fixed seeds where supported; report uncertainty, failures, p50/p95 latency, and total cost. 5. Ship only when the multi-agent design improves the primary quality or safety objective by a predeclared practically meaningful margin and stays within cost/latency limits. 6. Re-run the comparison after model, prompt, tool, topology, or workload changes. Tradeoffs Paired evaluation delays rollout and consumes inference budget. It prevents a permanently more expensive architecture based on anecdotes. Anti-patterns - Counting agent opinions as independent evidence when they share model, prompt, or retrieved sources. - Reporting only task accuracy while omitting cost, latency, variance, and catastrophic failures. - Selecting a framework first and inventing roles afterward. Enterprise Considerations Archive datasets, evaluator versions, raw traces, confidence intervals, and approval records. Segment results by tenant and risk tier; aggregate wins must not conceal regressions for protected or high-impact cohorts. Checklist - [ ] Single-agent control has equal resources. - [ ] Workload and practical improvement margin were predeclared. - [ ] Quality, safety, cost, latency, and variance are reported. - [ ] Evaluator leakage and correlated-agent evidence are controlled. - [ ] Re-evaluation triggers are configured. References - NIST AI RMF 1.0 - NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile - Multi-Agent Collaboration Mechanisms: A Survey (research survey; validate findings in-system) Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Cost, Budgets, and Termination
docs.description: Bound resource consumption and guarantee every multi-agent workflow reaches an explicit terminal outcome.
docs.text: Cost, Budgets, and Termination Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Bound resource consumption and guarantee every multi-agent workflow reaches an explicit terminal outcome. Why Per-call limits do not prevent fan-out, retries, recursive delegation, or unproductive debate from exhausting time and money. How 1. Allocate a workflow envelope for currency, tokens, tool calls, agents, concurrent branches, wall time, delegation depth, and retries. 2. Atomically reserve child budgets from the parent; unused amounts return, but children cannot mint budget. 3. Record actual and committed spend by task, tenant, model, tool, and agent. 4. Apply soft thresholds for adaptation and hard thresholds that reject new work and cancel safely. 5. Terminate on success criteria, deadline, cancellation, budget exhaustion, policy denial, repeated action/state digest, no measurable progress, or unrecoverable failure. 6. Propagate cancellation to descendants, revoke leases/tokens, compensate pending effects, checkpoint the terminal reason, and produce a partial-result manifest. 7. Alert on fan-out, retry, spend-rate, and zombie-work anomalies. Tradeoffs Hard budgets can stop tasks that would succeed with one more attempt. Explicit escalation and risk-tiered overrides are safer than unlimited automatic extension. Anti-patterns - Estimating cost only after completion. - Resetting retry or token counters when work moves to another agent. - Treating timeout as cancellation without stopping descendants and external jobs. Enterprise Considerations Enforce tenant quotas and chargeback tags. Financial limits must fail closed, overrides require accountable approval, and metering records must be reconciled with provider invoices. Checklist - [ ] Parent-to-child budget conservation is atomic. - [ ] Hard limits cover fan-out, retries, tools, time, and spend. - [ ] All terminal conditions and partial-result behavior are tested. - [ ] Cancellation revokes descendants, leases, and credentials. - [ ] Cost telemetry reconciles against provider billing. References - FinOps Framework: FinOps for AI - OpenTelemetry specification - NIST AI RMF 1.0 Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Durable State and Checkpoints
docs.description: Provide recoverable, conflict-safe workflow state independent of model context and worker lifetime.
docs.text: Durable State and Checkpoints Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Provide recoverable, conflict-safe workflow state independent of model context and worker lifetime. Why Agents retry, crash, duplicate messages, and race. A transcript cannot provide atomic transitions, exactly-once effects, schema migration, or deterministic recovery. How 1. Store authoritative state in a transactional system; workers receive immutable state snapshots and expected versions. 2. Model transitions as a state machine with terminal states succeeded, failed, cancelled, and expired. 3. Require compare-and-swap version checks, idempotency keys, outbox/inbox deduplication, and leases for exclusive work. 4. Checkpoint after validated boundaries and before irreversible effects. Include schema version, workflow definition digest, inputs, outputs, tool receipts, budget consumed, pending work, and provenance pointers. 5. Separate checkpoint creation from external side effects; use compensating transactions where atomic commit is impossible. 6. On resume, verify digests and compatibility, reacquire authorization, reconcile uncertain side effects, then continue from the last committed transition. 7. Test worker death, duplicate delivery, stale writes, partial writes, corrupt checkpoints, schema upgrades, and regional failover. Tradeoffs Fine-grained checkpoints improve recovery but increase storage and contention. Checkpoint only validated semantic boundaries, not every token or reasoning step. Anti-patterns - Last-write-wins state updates from multiple agents. - Replaying a tool call because a response was lost without checking its idempotency receipt. - Restoring old credentials, policy decisions, or budgets from a checkpoint. Enterprise Considerations Encrypt state, segregate tenants, classify checkpoint data, and apply retention/deletion policy. Recovery objectives must include the state store, artifact store, audit log, and identity dependencies. Checklist - [ ] State machine, invariants, schema versions, and terminal states are explicit. - [ ] Optimistic concurrency and idempotency are enforced. - [ ] Checkpoints carry provenance, budget, and workflow digests. - [ ] Resume re-authorizes and reconciles side effects. - [ ] Failure-injection and disaster-recovery tests pass. References - AWS Builders’ Library: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs - CloudEvents 1.0 specification - NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, Contingency Planning Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Agent Identity and Authenticated Delegation
docs.description: Bind every agent action to a verifiable workload identity and a constrained delegation chain.
docs.text: Agent Identity and Authenticated Delegation Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Bind every agent action to a verifiable workload identity and a constrained delegation chain. Why Agent names in prompts are labels, not identities. Without cryptographic authentication and least-privilege delegation, a peer can impersonate a supervisor or amplify the caller's authority. How 1. Issue short-lived workload credentials from the platform identity provider; prohibit shared secrets and static agent API keys. 2. Bind each identity to code/config digest, environment, tenant, owner, and allowed tools. 3. Exchange the caller credential for an audience-restricted delegation token containing iss, sub, aud, exp, jti, task ID, permitted actions, resource scope, and parent delegation hash. 4. Re-authorize at every hop against the original user intent and current policy. Never infer authority from message text. 5. Reject token forwarding, audience mismatch, expired/replayed IDs, excessive delegation depth, or capabilities broader than the parent grant. 6. Revoke active sessions and rotate keys when an identity, prompt, tool, or runtime is compromised. Tradeoffs Per-hop token exchange adds latency and identity infrastructure. It sharply limits confused-deputy and privilege-propagation blast radius. Anti-patterns - Reusing the user's bearer token across workers. - Treating an agent ID, role prompt, or mTLS connection alone as authorization. - Allowing a delegate to create grants it does not possess. Enterprise Considerations Use hardware-backed keys where risk warrants it, centralize policy decisions, record policy version and reason, and separate production identities from development. Human users remain accountable for approved high-impact delegation. Checklist - [ ] Workload identity is cryptographically verified. - [ ] Tokens are short-lived, audience-bound, replay-resistant, and task-scoped. - [ ] Every hop attenuates or preserves—not expands—privilege. - [ ] Delegation depth and emergency revocation are enforced. - [ ] Authorization is tested independently of natural-language instructions. References - NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture - RFC 8693, OAuth 2.0 Token Exchange - SPIFFE specification Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Message Provenance and Non-Repudiation
docs.description: Make agent messages attributable, integrity-protected, replay-resistant, and auditable.
docs.text: Message Provenance and Non-Repudiation Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Make agent messages attributable, integrity-protected, replay-resistant, and auditable. Why Transport encryption does not prove which workload created a stored message. Operational non-repudiation requires signed content plus protected keys and tamper-evident retention; signatures alone cannot establish truth. How Use a canonical, versioned envelope: 1. Canonicalize and hash the body and artifact manifest; sign protected routing fields and digest using an approved algorithm and key ID. 2. Verify identity, audience, signature, time window, nonce, schema, delegation chain, and content digest before processing. 3. Persist accepted/rejected verification outcomes in an append-only, hash-chained log with trusted timestamps. 4. Keep original bytes and transformation records; derived summaries never replace source evidence. 5. Define key rotation, compromise, algorithm migration, and evidentiary export procedures. Tradeoffs Signing and immutable retention add storage, key-management, and privacy obligations. Redact before signing or preserve authorized encrypted originals; post-signature editing invalidates evidence. Anti-patterns - Signing only the body while leaving sender, recipient, task, or expiry mutable. - Calling a database audit row “non-repudiation” without protected signing keys and tamper evidence. - Assuming a valid signature means content is correct or authorized. Enterprise Considerations Align retention and legal admissibility with counsel. Restrict audit access, encrypt sensitive payloads, and preserve verification software, trust roots, and policy versions for the retention period. Checklist - [ ] Canonical envelope and artifact digests are versioned. - [ ] Signatures cover routing, time, delegation, and content. - [ ] Replay and clock-skew tests pass. - [ ] Audit records are append-only and tamper-evident. - [ ] Key compromise and evidentiary export drills pass. References - RFC 9421, HTTP Message Signatures - RFC 8785, JSON Canonicalization Scheme - NIST SP 800-57 Part 1 Rev. 5 Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Multi-Agent Threat Controls
docs.description: Control loop, collusion, confused-deputy, prompt-injection, and privilege-propagation risks unique to delegated agent execution.
docs.text: Multi-Agent Threat Controls Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Control loop, collusion, confused-deputy, prompt-injection, and privilege-propagation risks unique to delegated agent execution. Why Agent messages and retrieved artifacts are untrusted input. Repetition can amplify an error into actions across multiple identities, while apparent consensus may be correlated or malicious. How Risk Prevent Detect Recover --- --- --- --- Loop DAG/depth constraints, iteration budget, idempotency repeated state/action digest, no-progress counter cancel branch, restore checkpoint, escalate Collusion/correlated error independent evidence, role separation, deterministic gates source-overlap and anomalous agreement checks quarantine agents and re-evaluate from trusted evidence Confused deputy re-authorize original intent at every tool call requested action/resource differs from grant deny, revoke delegation, investigate trace Privilege propagation capability attenuation and audience-bound tokens downstream grant exceeds parent reject chain and revoke descendants Indirect injection treat messages/documents as data; isolate privileged executor instruction-like content, intent drift quarantine source, rotate affected state, replay safely Use an external policy enforcement point for tools and state writes. High-impact actions require deterministic validation and independent approval; an LLM critique is not an authorization control. Tradeoffs Isolation and independent approval reduce autonomy and throughput. They are mandatory where a compromise can create irreversible, cross-tenant, financial, security, or safety impact. Anti-patterns - Majority voting among replicas of the same model as proof. - Letting workers modify system prompts, policy, identity, budgets, or termination rules. - Passing raw peer messages directly into a privileged agent's instruction channel. Enterprise Considerations Threat-model trust boundaries and supply chains, map alerts to incident response, and preserve the full delegation/provenance graph. Run adversarial exercises across tenants and compromised-agent scenarios. Checklist - [ ] No-progress, repeat-action, depth, and cycle detectors terminate execution. - [ ] Privilege cannot increase down a delegation chain. - [ ] Original user intent is available to every policy decision. - [ ] Peer content is untrusted and instruction/data boundaries are enforced. - [ ] Compromised-agent containment and replay are exercised. References - OWASP LLM Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet - OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 - NIST SP 800-207, Zero Trust Architecture Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Knowledge Graph Construction
docs.description: Construct relationship-centric knowledge with explicit ontology, provenance, and review.
docs.text: Knowledge Graph Construction Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Maturity: Emerging for LLM-assisted construction Purpose Construct relationship-centric knowledge with explicit ontology, provenance, and review. Why Graphs help multi-hop, entity, and relationship queries, but LLM extraction can create plausible unsupported edges at scale. How Start only after relationship-heavy queries beat document retrieval in a pilot. Define competency questions and a versioned ontology; assign stable entity IDs. Extract candidate entities/relations with source spans, confidence, extractor version, tenant/ACL, and valid time. Validate schema deterministically, reconcile entities conservatively, and require human or trusted-rule approval for high-impact edges. Publish immutable graph versions and rollback manifests. Tradeoffs Graphs improve explicit traversal and conflict representation but add ontology, entity-resolution, and stewardship cost. Keep source documents authoritative. Anti-patterns - Creating edges without source-span provenance. - Global fuzzy entity merges. - Building a graph because it appears more advanced than hybrid search. Enterprise Considerations Tenant-scope nodes and edges, govern ontology changes, and audit merges/splits. LLM-generated graph construction remains emerging and requires corpus-specific validation. Checklist - [ ] Competency questions justify the graph. - [ ] Ontology and entity identity are versioned. - [ ] Every edge has source, time, ACL, and extraction provenance. - [ ] Merge, rollback, and correction tests pass. References - W3C RDF 1.1 Concepts - W3C PROV-O - GraphRAG paper (emerging research) Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial emerging-practice standard.

docs.title: Knowledge Graph Maintenance
docs.description: Keep graph knowledge current, correctable, and reconstructable as sources and ontologies change.
docs.text: Knowledge Graph Maintenance Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Maturity: Emerging for automated repair Purpose Keep graph knowledge current, correctable, and reconstructable as sources and ontologies change. Why Stale edges and bad entity merges spread errors across many answers. Graph derivatives must never outlive source corrections or deletions. How Use append/version semantics with valid and transaction time. Process source changes through lineage-aware deltas; tombstone descendants on deletion. Version ontology and migration code, detect orphaned nodes, contradictory edges, merge anomalies, provenance gaps, and ACL drift. Rebuild from authoritative sources on corruption and compare graph/query regressions before promotion. Tradeoffs Incremental maintenance is faster but complex; full rebuilds are simpler and safer but expensive. Maintain both a delta path and tested rebuild path. Anti-patterns - In-place edge mutation without history. - Manual graph fixes that do not correct the source pipeline. - Automated entity merge repair without review. Enterprise Considerations Assign ontology and domain stewards, publish freshness/deletion SLOs, and retain migration/audit evidence. Automated LLM repair remains emerging. Checklist - [ ] Temporal/version semantics and lineage are enforced. - [ ] Corrections/deletions propagate to all graph descendants. - [ ] Integrity, ACL-drift, and contradiction monitors run. - [ ] Rebuild and ontology rollback are tested. References - W3C PROV-O - W3C OWL 2 Overview Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial emerging-practice standard.

docs.title: Knowledge Graph Querying
docs.description: Use graph traversal safely for entity, relationship, temporal, and multi-hop retrieval.
docs.text: Knowledge Graph Querying Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Maturity: Emerging for LLM-generated queries Purpose Use graph traversal safely for entity, relationship, temporal, and multi-hop retrieval. Why Graph retrieval can answer queries poorly served by lexical or vector search, but unconstrained generated queries can leak data or produce expensive traversals. How Map each validated query class to parameterized templates or a constrained query AST. Resolve entities within tenant scope, apply node/edge ACL and temporal predicates before traversal, enforce path depth/cardinality/cost limits, and return source-backed subgraphs. If an LLM proposes a query, parse, authorize, estimate, and execute it through a read-only gateway. Evaluate against vector/keyword baselines. Tradeoffs Templates are safer and predictable but less flexible. Generated graph queries remain emerging and require a sandbox and deterministic policy. Anti-patterns - Executing raw model-generated Cypher/SPARQL. - Applying ACL only to final nodes. - Presenting a path as causal evidence without source support. Enterprise Considerations Use read replicas, workload limits, tenant partitions, query audit logs, and denial-of-wallet alerts. Checklist - [ ] Traversal is ACL- and time-filtered at every hop. - [ ] Queries are parameterized, bounded, and read-only. - [ ] Returned edges resolve to authorized evidence. - [ ] Graph retrieval demonstrates benefit per query class. References - W3C SPARQL 1.1 Query - OWASP Query Parameterization Cheat Sheet Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial emerging-practice standard.

docs.title: Episodic Memory
docs.description: Store attributable records of past events and decisions for later task-relevant recall.
docs.text: Episodic Memory Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Store attributable records of past events and decisions for later task-relevant recall. Why Raw conversation history is noisy and privacy-heavy; model-generated recollections can convert inference into false fact. How Write episodes only after a defined event boundary. Store event time, observed time, participants, tenant/ACL, source pointers, outcome, confidence, supersession, retention, and extractor version. Separate observed facts from model interpretations. Retrieve by authorized scope, temporal constraints, entities, and relevance; surface conflicts and source evidence. Correct or delete via lineage. Tradeoffs Curated episodes are more reliable than transcripts but may omit nuance. Preserve source pointers and allow abstention when evidence is incomplete. Anti-patterns - Saving every turn as permanent memory. - Writing an agent’s summary as a verified fact. - Retrieving stale episodes without effective-time filters. Enterprise Considerations Episodes often contain personal data. Enforce purpose limitation, subject access, retention, correction, and deletion across derivatives. Checklist - [ ] Fact and inference fields are separate. - [ ] Event/effective times and provenance are retained. - [ ] ACL, retention, conflict, correction, and deletion paths work. - [ ] Recall usefulness and harmful-memory rates are evaluated. References - W3C PROV-O - NIST Privacy Framework 1.0 Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: External Durable Memory
docs.description: Store cross-session facts, preferences, and task state in durable systems with transactional governance.
docs.text: External Durable Memory Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Store cross-session facts, preferences, and task state in durable systems with transactional governance. Why External persistence survives context and process failure, but broad shared stores create stale-write, tenant-leakage, and deletion risks. How Separate authoritative task state from recall-oriented memory. Use typed schemas, tenant keys, row-level authorization, optimistic concurrency, idempotent writes, encryption, audit events, retention, and backup/restore. Require explicit write criteria and validation; agent outputs enter a pending state until policy approves them. Maintain lineage to every cache, index, and summary. Tradeoffs Transactional stores improve correctness but do not provide semantic retrieval by themselves. Add indexes as replaceable derivatives, never as the sole record. Anti-patterns - A shared vector store as authoritative state. - Unversioned upserts and last-write-wins preferences. - Backups that cannot honor deletion or tenant restore boundaries. Enterprise Considerations Define RPO/RTO, residency, key ownership, legal hold, deletion, and tenant-level restore. Exercise failover and corrupt-index rebuilds. Checklist - [ ] Authoritative and derived stores are distinguished. - [ ] Transactions, versions, idempotency, and audit are enforced. - [ ] Tenant isolation and deletion include backups and derivatives. - [ ] Restore and re-index drills pass. References - NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: In-Context Working Memory
docs.description: Manage ephemeral task context and compaction without making the model context authoritative state.
docs.text: In-Context Working Memory Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Manage ephemeral task context and compaction without making the model context authoritative state. Why Context is bounded, order-sensitive, and exposed to untrusted retrieved content. Summarization can silently remove constraints, negation, and provenance. How Assemble context from authenticated instructions, immutable task state, authorized evidence, and recent interactions with explicit delimiters and provenance. Reserve capacity using measured model/task behavior. Compact at evaluation-derived thresholds into a structured summary containing objectives, decisions, constraints, entities, quantities, unresolved items, permissions, source pointers, and summary lineage; retain authoritative originals outside the prompt. Run compaction-loss tests before replacing context. Tradeoffs More verbatim context preserves detail but increases cost and distraction. Structured compaction saves tokens but requires validation and reversible source references. Anti-patterns - Fixed universal token or “last N messages” rules. - Destructive summary replacement without replay tests. - Mixing retrieved data into the instruction channel. Enterprise Considerations Apply classification, redaction, tenant boundaries, and no-log rules before prompt assembly. Provider retention settings do not replace application governance. Checklist - [ ] Context sources are authorized and attributable. - [ ] Durable state remains external. - [ ] Compaction is structured, reversible, and evaluated. - [ ] Prompt logs follow retention and tenant policy. References - OWASP Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet - Lost in the Middle (research evidence; measure on selected models) Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Procedural Memory
docs.description: Govern reusable prompts, skills, policies, and workflows as executable production artifacts.
docs.text: Procedural Memory Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Govern reusable prompts, skills, policies, and workflows as executable production artifacts. Why Procedures influence actions and privileges. Unreviewed self-modification turns model output or poisoned memory into executable policy. How Store procedures in version control with owner, trigger, inputs/outputs, required capabilities, constraints, failure handling, tests, approval, expiry, and artifact signature. Execute only approved immutable versions. Propose changes through review and isolated evaluation; never let an agent overwrite its active procedure. Record the procedure digest in each run. Tradeoffs Review slows adaptation but enables reproducibility, rollback, and separation of duties. Anti-patterns - Automatically promoting “successful” traces into production skills. - Embedding credentials or tenant data in procedures. - Allowing runtime prompt edits to bypass release controls. Enterprise Considerations Treat procedural memory as software supply chain material: signed releases, protected branches, dependency review, least privilege, and emergency revocation. Checklist - [ ] Procedure owner, version, signature, and required capabilities are recorded. - [ ] Tests cover success, failure, injection, and rollback. - [ ] Runtime self-modification is prohibited. - [ ] Every execution records the immutable digest. References - SLSA specification - NIST SP 800-218, Secure Software Development Framework Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Semantic Memory
docs.description: Serve governed factual and conceptual knowledge with source-level attribution and temporal validity.
docs.text: Semantic Memory Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Serve governed factual and conceptual knowledge with source-level attribution and temporal validity. Why Semantic memory becomes dangerous when extracted claims lose their source, scope, qualifiers, or effective dates. How Ingest authoritative sources through validation and provenance capture. Represent claims with subject, predicate, object/value, qualifiers, valid time, source version, confidence, ACL, and supersession. Keep extracted claims linked to source spans. Resolve conflicts by documented source authority and time; return multiple claims or abstain when unresolved. Rebuild derivatives after corrections. Tradeoffs Normalized claims support precise retrieval and conflict handling but require extraction and stewardship. Source chunks are simpler but make entity and temporal reasoning harder. Anti-patterns - Treating embedding similarity as factual confidence. - Flattening conflicting claims into one “canonical” answer without policy. - Dropping qualifiers during extraction. Enterprise Considerations Assign domain owners and authority tiers. Version taxonomies, preserve lineage, and audit corrections affecting regulated decisions. Checklist - [ ] Claims retain source spans, qualifiers, and effective time. - [ ] Authority and conflict policies are explicit. - [ ] Corrections propagate to indexes and answers. - [ ] Unsupported claims trigger abstention. References - W3C PROV-O - W3C RDF 1.1 Concepts Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Advanced RAG
docs.description: Add query transformation, multi-query retrieval, reranking, and contextual assembly only where baseline error analysis justifies them.
docs.text: Advanced RAG Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Add query transformation, multi-query retrieval, reranking, and contextual assembly only where baseline error analysis justifies them. Why Advanced stages can improve hard queries but also distort intent, multiply cost, and hide authorization or provenance failures. How Classify baseline failures; add one versioned stage at a time and run ablations. Preserve the original query and authenticated scope through rewriting. Generate bounded variants, retrieve each under identical ACLs, fuse/deduplicate, rerank authorized candidates, and enforce evidence/citation checks. Cap expansion, latency, tokens, and retries; fall back to baseline or abstain on stage failure. Tradeoffs Reranking and expansion improve selected query classes at higher latency and provider exposure. Use smaller deterministic stages where they meet the gate. Anti-patterns - Letting a rewrite change tenant, time range, or requested action. - Adding components without ablation results. - Treating reranker score as factual support. Enterprise Considerations Audit every transformation, review provider data handling for each stage, and monitor segmented regressions and denial-of-wallet attacks. Checklist - [ ] Each stage maps to measured baseline failures. - [ ] Original intent and ACL scope are immutable. - [ ] Ablation proves incremental quality within budgets. - [ ] Failure fallback and citation verification pass. References - Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels (HyDE) (research technique; evaluate locally) - BEIR benchmark Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Agentic RAG
docs.description: Govern agent-directed retrieval planning for queries that deterministic pipelines cannot handle within requirements.
docs.text: Agentic RAG Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Maturity: Emerging Purpose Govern agent-directed retrieval planning for queries that deterministic pipelines cannot handle within requirements. Why An agent can iteratively decompose and inspect evidence, but also amplifies prompt injection, cost, loops, and unauthorized query generation. How First prove failure of baseline and advanced deterministic RAG. Give the planner read-only, least-privilege retrieval tools with immutable tenant/ACL scope. Use typed plans, bounded subqueries, source allowlists, loop/no-progress detection, per-step evidence ledgers, total budgets, and explicit termination. Separate the untrusted-content reader from any privileged actor. Validate the final claim-evidence graph and citations before response. Tradeoffs Agentic retrieval adapts to novel multi-step questions but is slower, less reproducible, and harder to secure. Keep it behind a routed, evaluated path and a deterministic fallback. Anti-patterns - Giving a retrieval agent general-purpose tools or write access. - Letting retrieved instructions alter the plan or authorization scope. - Shipping because a few demos outperform fixed RAG. Enterprise Considerations Require risk approval, full step-level traces, cost quotas, incident kill switches, and periodic benefit revalidation. The pattern remains emerging. Checklist - [ ] Deterministic alternatives failed documented query classes. - [ ] Tools are read-only, scoped, and independently authorized. - [ ] Budgets, loop detection, termination, and fallback are enforced. - [ ] Claim-level citation and adversarial tests pass. References - OWASP Prompt Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet - ReAct (research pattern; not a security control) Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial emerging-practice standard.

docs.title: Hybrid RAG
docs.description: Fuse complementary retrieval modes when workload evidence shows that one mode is insufficient.
docs.text: Hybrid RAG Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Fuse complementary retrieval modes when workload evidence shows that one mode is insufficient. Why Lexical and dense retrieval often fail on different queries; graph retrieval may add value for explicit relationship questions. None is universally required. How Establish per-mode baselines, then run complementarity and ablation analysis by query class. Execute only justified retrievers under identical pre-retrieval ACL/time filters. Fuse with a documented method such as reciprocal rank fusion, deduplicate source versions, rerank, enforce context diversity and token budget, and verify citations. Route simple query classes to one mode to control latency. Tradeoffs Hybrid retrieval may improve coverage but increases infrastructure, tuning, latency, and incident surface. Graph retrieval is an emerging optional branch, not part of the minimum definition. Anti-patterns - Claiming universal recall gains or fixed percentages. - Sending every query to every index. - Fusing candidates before each retriever enforces authorization. Enterprise Considerations Apply consistent deletion and correction across all indexes, record per-retriever provenance, and reconcile tenant isolation and residency controls. Checklist - [ ] Complementary errors justify each retriever. - [ ] ACL and lifecycle controls are equivalent across indexes. - [ ] Fusion, routing, and reranking are versioned. - [ ] Ablation, latency, cost, and citation gates pass. References - Reciprocal Rank Fusion - BEIR benchmark Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Replaced universal hybrid mandate with evidence-based fusion.

docs.title: Baseline RAG
docs.description: Define the minimum retrieval-generation baseline used before adding rewriting, fusion, graphs, or agents.
docs.text: Baseline RAG Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define the minimum retrieval-generation baseline used before adding rewriting, fusion, graphs, or agents. Why A simple, observable baseline exposes whether complexity produces real value and localizes retrieval versus generation failures. How Authenticate the principal, derive tenant/ACL scope, retrieve from one evaluated index with predicates applied in the datastore, assemble bounded source-labelled context, require answer/abstain behavior, and emit citations to immutable source versions. Log query, policy, index, retriever, candidates, scores, prompt template, model, answer, and citation verification under privacy policy. Tradeoffs The baseline is easy to test and operate but can miss mixed lexical/semantic or multi-hop queries. Keep it as the control even after advanced paths ship. Anti-patterns - Calling post-retrieval filtering authorization. - Returning an answer when authorized evidence is absent. - Evaluating only end-answer quality. Enterprise Considerations Apply tenant isolation, data minimization, retention, deletion, source licensing, and provider data-processing controls. Checklist - [ ] ACL is enforced before retrieval. - [ ] Every result and citation resolves to a source version. - [ ] Retrieval and generation traces are reproducible. - [ ] Unanswerable and cross-tenant tests pass. References - Retrieval-Augmented Generation - OWASP RAG Security Cheat Sheet Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production baseline.

docs.title: Level 6: Memory and Knowledge Systems
docs.description: Define production memory and retrieval systems that are attributable, tenant-safe, correctable, deletable, and measurably useful.
docs.text: Level 6: Memory and Knowledge Systems Version: 2.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Prerequisite: governed identity, authorization, and evaluation infrastructure Purpose Define production memory and retrieval systems that are attributable, tenant-safe, correctable, deletable, and measurably useful. Why Memory can preserve mistakes, secrets, stale claims, and injected instructions as efficiently as it preserves useful knowledge. Retrieval quality and control must be measured on the actual corpus and workload; universal recall percentages, chunk overlaps, vector-count cutoffs, and compression thresholds are unsupported. How 1. Govern the memory lifecycle and security and poisoning controls. 2. Select memory by semantics: in-context, episodic, semantic, procedural, or external state. 3. Select and combine retrieval modes from measured query classes, not ideology. 4. Enforce authorization before candidate retrieval and again before generation. 5. Validate with retrieval and citation evaluation. Corpus Knowledge Graphs - Construction - Querying - Maintenance Vector and Retrieval Infrastructure - Store selection - Indexing patterns - Retrieval optimization RAG Architectures - Naive RAG - Advanced RAG - Hybrid RAG - Agentic RAG Tradeoffs Stronger provenance, isolation, and deletion add metadata and operational cost. Hybrid and graph retrieval can improve specific query classes but increase latency and tuning surface; they are enabled only when offline and online evidence justifies them. Anti-patterns - Write-only memory: no expiry, correction, conflict, or deletion path. - ACL after retrieval: unauthorized candidates can leak through ranking, caches, telemetry, or timing. - Similarity as truth: high vector score does not establish authority, freshness, or factual support. - Summary replacement: destructive compaction silently removes commitments and qualifiers. - Graph by default: knowledge graphs remain an emerging option for relationship-heavy workloads, not a universal RAG requirement. Enterprise Considerations Classify data before ingestion; enforce purpose, residency, legal hold, retention, deletion, correction, and tenant isolation across source, indexes, caches, replicas, backups, traces, and derived artifacts. Checklist - [ ] Every record has source, owner, tenant, ACL, version, timestamps, and transformation provenance. - [ ] Retention, deletion, correction, conflict, and legal-hold workflows are tested end to end. - [ ] Authorization occurs before retrieval and cache access. - [ ] Poisoning detection, quarantine, rollback, and re-index recovery are exercised. - [ ] Retrieval mode is selected per evaluated query class. - [ ] Retrieval, generation, citation support, and compaction-loss tests pass workload-specific gates. References - NIST AI RMF 1.0 - NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 - OWASP RAG Security Cheat Sheet - Retrieval-Augmented Generation Changelog - 2.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Added lifecycle, provenance, isolation, correction, poisoning, retrieval-selection, ACL-first, citation, and compaction standards; removed unsupported numeric mandates.

docs.title: Memory Lifecycle Governance
docs.description: Control memory from authorized creation through correction, expiry, deletion, and verifiable destruction.
docs.text: Memory Lifecycle Governance Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Control memory from authorized creation through correction, expiry, deletion, and verifiable destruction. Why Persistent memory creates privacy, stale-data, and accountability risk unless every derived copy can be found and governed. How 1. At ingestion record immutable source ID/version, tenant, subject, owner, purpose, ACL, classification, consent/legal basis where applicable, timestamps, content hash, parser/embedding versions, and derivation lineage. 2. Validate, scan, and stage records before publication; never learn directly from model output without approval. 3. Resolve conflicts using source authority, effective time, and explicit supersession. Preserve competing claims when no policy resolves them; do not let recency or similarity silently win. 4. Set retention and review dates by class. Expire access automatically; legal hold prevents destruction but not correction annotations. 5. Propagate correction/deletion tombstones to chunks, embeddings, graphs, caches, replicas, summaries, evaluation sets, and eligible backups; verify completion. 6. Keep minimal non-content audit evidence when law and policy permit, and provide data-subject/tenant exports. Tradeoffs Lineage and deletion propagation cost storage and engineering effort. They are prerequisites for trustworthy correction and defensible retention. Anti-patterns - “Indefinite” as a default retention class. - Updating source text while leaving old embeddings and cached answers active. - Resolving conflict by whichever result ranks first. Enterprise Considerations Map controls to privacy, records, residency, discovery, and legal-hold obligations. Assign data stewards and publish deletion SLOs with exception evidence. Checklist - [ ] Provenance and derivation lineage are complete. - [ ] Retention, review, legal hold, correction, and deletion are policy-driven. - [ ] Conflict decisions are deterministic and auditable. - [ ] Tombstones reach every derivative and cache. - [ ] Deletion and correction drills satisfy SLOs. References - NIST Privacy Framework 1.0 - NIST SP 800-88 Rev. 1, Media Sanitization - W3C PROV-O Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Retrieval, Citation, and Compaction Evaluation
docs.description: Define workload-specific evidence for retrieval quality, citation support, and memory-compaction safety.
docs.text: Retrieval, Citation, and Compaction Evaluation Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define workload-specific evidence for retrieval quality, citation support, and memory-compaction safety. Why No universal recall threshold or framework score proves production readiness. Metrics depend on corpus, query distribution, risk, annotation quality, and the cost of misses. How 1. Create versioned, adjudicated query sets covering answerable, unanswerable, exact identifier, semantic, temporal, relationship, multilingual, ACL, stale, conflicting, and adversarial cases. 2. Evaluate retrieval separately with recall@k, precision@k, MRR/nDCG where relevant, latency, cost, ACL violations, freshness, and abstention behavior. 3. Evaluate generation for claim correctness, completeness, unsupported-claim rate, and source use; do not collapse all stages into one judge score. 4. Verify each citation deterministically resolves to an authorized source/version, then evaluate whether cited spans entail each material claim. Sample human review and calibrate model judges against it. 5. For compaction, replay tasks before/after compression and test retention of commitments, constraints, unresolved questions, entities, dates, quantities, provenance, permissions, and safety instructions. Measure omission, contradiction, and task-success delta. 6. Set gates from risk appetite and baseline performance; publish confidence intervals and segment results. Run offline gates on every material change and online canaries with rollback. Tradeoffs High-quality labels are expensive and evolve with the corpus. They are more reliable than arbitrary percentages or uncalibrated LLM judges. Anti-patterns - Using answer fluency as retrieval evaluation. - Verifying only that a citation URL exists. - Testing summaries with generic similarity, which can hide lost negation or numbers. Enterprise Considerations Protect evaluation data from training leakage, report tenant/cohort performance, retain evaluator versions, and require domain experts for high-impact claims. Checklist - [ ] Query set covers ACL, conflict, freshness, and adversarial cases. - [ ] Retrieval and generation are evaluated independently. - [ ] Citations resolve and support material claims. - [ ] Judge calibration and human sampling are documented. - [ ] Compaction loss and rollback gates pass. References - BEIR benchmark - RAGAS (evaluation method; calibrate before use) - NIST AI 600-1, Generative AI Profile Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Memory Security and Poisoning Recovery
docs.description: Prevent cross-tenant disclosure and detect, contain, and recover from poisoned memory or retrieval indexes.
docs.text: Memory Security and Poisoning Recovery Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Prevent cross-tenant disclosure and detect, contain, and recover from poisoned memory or retrieval indexes. Why Post-retrieval filtering is too late: unauthorized candidates may enter caches, rerankers, prompts, traces, or side channels. Poisoned content can persist and repeatedly steer privileged agents. How 1. Derive tenant and principal scope from authenticated identity, never request text. 2. Enforce row/document ACLs in the datastore query before vector, keyword, or graph traversal; fail closed when policy metadata is missing. 3. Use tenant-separated encryption, namespaces/partitions, cache keys, quotas, and telemetry. Test isolation with canary records. 4. Admit content through source allowlists, signature/hash verification, parser sandboxing, malware/injection scans, anomaly detection, and steward approval by risk tier. 5. Monitor source churn, embedding-neighborhood anomalies, unusual retrieval frequency, instruction-like content, and answer drift. 6. On detection: stop ingestion, quarantine source and descendants, revoke caches, identify lineage, restore a known-good snapshot, rebuild all affected indexes, replay verified deltas, and regression-test before release. Tradeoffs Physical tenant separation costs more but reduces blast radius. Shared indexes are acceptable only with datastore-enforced predicates and proven isolation under failure. Anti-patterns - Metadata filtering performed in application code after top-k retrieval. - Deleting only the source document while poisoned embeddings or graph edges remain. - Treating prompt-injection classification as a complete security boundary. Enterprise Considerations Integrate alerts with incident response, preserve chain of custody, notify affected tenants under policy, and rotate credentials if poisoned content triggered actions. Checklist - [ ] ACL predicates execute before all retrieval paths. - [ ] Caches, logs, and observability are tenant-scoped. - [ ] Ingestion provenance and quarantine gates are enforced. - [ ] Poisoning lineage and known-good snapshots are available. - [ ] Cross-tenant and poisoning-recovery exercises pass. References - OWASP RAG Security Cheat Sheet - OWASP LLM08: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses - NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Indexing Patterns
docs.description: Create reconstructable lexical, vector, and graph derivatives without losing provenance or access policy.
docs.text: Indexing Patterns Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Create reconstructable lexical, vector, and graph derivatives without losing provenance or access policy. Why Chunk size, overlap, and embedding choice are corpus-dependent. Arbitrary defaults can split evidence, duplicate noise, or prevent exact correction. How Parse into logical units before token limits; preserve headings, tables, code, page/span offsets, and parent-child relationships. Assign stable source/chunk/version IDs and store tenant, ACL, classification, effective time, hash, parser, embedding model, and lineage. Tune chunking/overlap on retrieval evaluation; overlap is not mandatory when semantic boundaries preserve context. Stage and validate new index versions, then atomically switch aliases. Keep a full rebuild path. Tradeoffs Smaller chunks improve precision but lose context; larger chunks preserve context but consume prompt budget. Parent-child retrieval can balance both at added complexity. Anti-patterns - Mandating a fixed percentage overlap. - Updating embeddings without recording model/version or re-evaluating. - Indexing documents whose ACL or provenance is missing. Enterprise Considerations Scan parsers and source formats, encrypt derivatives, scope queues and caches by tenant, and include index versions in legal hold/deletion workflows. Checklist - [ ] Logical structure and source offsets are preserved. - [ ] IDs, ACLs, hashes, versions, and lineage are complete. - [ ] Chunking is selected by evaluation. - [ ] Atomic rollout, rollback, deletion, and rebuild are tested. References - W3C PROV-O - OWASP RAG Security Cheat Sheet Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production standard.

docs.title: Retrieval Optimization and Mode Selection
docs.description: Select vector, keyword, graph, and fused retrieval by evaluated query class.
docs.text: Retrieval Optimization and Mode Selection Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Select vector, keyword, graph, and fused retrieval by evaluated query class. Why No retrieval mode dominates all workloads. Exact identifiers favor lexical search, paraphrases favor dense retrieval, and explicit multi-hop relationships may favor graphs. How Mode Select for Primary failure --- --- --- Keyword/BM25 identifiers, names, quoted text, rare terms vocabulary mismatch Dense vector semantic similarity, paraphrase exactness, freshness, opaque neighbors Graph explicit entity relations and bounded multi-hop ontology/edge quality and cost Hybrid fusion mixed query classes with measured complementary errors latency and tuning complexity Route only with a deterministic classifier or validated query features. Apply ACL/time filters inside each retriever, normalize/fuse scores with a versioned method, rerank authorized candidates, deduplicate by source, and tune top-k/reranking using segmented evaluation. Fall back or abstain when confidence and evidence are insufficient. Tradeoffs Fusion can improve robustness but costs more. Add each retriever only when its incremental quality exceeds its latency and operational budget. Anti-patterns - “Hybrid by default” without ablation evidence. - Comparing incomparable raw scores across retrievers. - Optimizing average recall while exact-ID or ACL cases fail. Enterprise Considerations Budget per tenant and query class, log routing/fusion versions, and monitor drift, cost, and unauthorized-candidate counts. Checklist - [ ] Query taxonomy and per-mode baselines exist. - [ ] ACL and temporal filters precede scoring. - [ ] Fusion/reranking is versioned and ablated. - [ ] Quality, latency, cost, and abstention gates pass by segment. References - BEIR benchmark - Reciprocal Rank Fusion Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial retrieval-selection standard.

docs.title: Retrieval Store Selection Guide
docs.description: Select vector infrastructure from measured workload, control, and lifecycle requirements.
docs.text: Retrieval Store Selection Guide Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Select vector infrastructure from measured workload, control, and lifecycle requirements. Why Vector count alone does not determine a product or migration threshold. Filtering selectivity, update rate, latency, recall, tenancy, operations, and compliance dominate. How Benchmark shortlisted stores with production-shaped vectors, metadata, ACL predicates, churn, concurrency, and failure modes. Gate on filtered retrieval quality, p95/p99 latency, ingest/delete/correction lag, backup/restore, tenant isolation, encryption/key control, observability, portability, and total cost. Start with the existing transactional platform only when it meets gates; select a specialized service when evidence shows a gap. Tradeoffs Integrated stores simplify consistency and operations. Specialized stores can improve scale or ANN features but add distributed lifecycle and vendor risk. Anti-patterns - Universal cutoffs such as “migrate at N vectors.” - Selecting from vendor feature matrices without corpus benchmarks. - Ignoring exact deletion, filtered recall, or restore behavior. Enterprise Considerations Review residency, subprocessors, private networking, key ownership, auditability, export format, disaster recovery, and contract exit. Checklist - [ ] Benchmark uses production corpus, filters, churn, and concurrency. - [ ] Quality, latency, lifecycle lag, cost, and isolation gates are set. - [ ] Restore, deletion, and portability are proven. - [ ] Selection ADR records evidence and re-evaluation triggers. References - PostgreSQL pgvector - ANN Benchmarks methodology (comparative benchmark; reproduce on own workload) - NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 Changelog - 1.0.0 — 2026-07-16: Replaced vendor/count mandates with workload evidence.

docs.title: LLM Caching Strategies
docs.description: Use exact, semantic, and provider caching without serving stale, cross-tenant, or unauthorized outputs.
docs.text: LLM Caching Strategies Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Use exact, semantic, and provider caching without serving stale, cross-tenant, or unauthorized outputs. Why Caching changes data flow and correctness, not just performance. When Use for repeatable, non-personalized workloads with explicit freshness. How 1. Classify cacheability by task and data. 2. Build keys from tenant, prompt release, model envelope, policy, locale, and source version. 3. Encrypt values and enforce tenant isolation. 4. Set TTL and event-driven invalidation. 5. Measure hit quality; purge on incident, deletion request, or policy change. Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Key specification - Isolation test - Freshness test - Purge evidence Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Tradeoffs Choice Benefit Cost --- --- --- Semantic cache Higher hit rate False-equivalence risk Exact cache Predictable Lower hit rate Anti-patterns - Caching personalized responses globally. - Ignoring deletion propagation. Enterprise considerations - Document cache as a data store. - Apply legal hold and deletion consistently. Control mapping Source Practical mapping Claim boundary --- --- --- NIST AI RMF Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage evidence Alignment aid; not NIST approval ISO/IEC 42001 and 23894 Management-system and AI-risk control inputs No certification is asserted OWASP GenAI Threat scenarios and verification cases Coverage does not prove security Checklist - [ ] Tenant boundary tested. - [ ] Invalidation works. - [ ] Sensitive tasks default off. References - NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and Generative AI Profile (accessed 2026-07-16). - ISO, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and ISO/IEC 23894:2023 (accessed 2026-07-16). Mapping indicates control alignment only; it is not a certification claim. - OWASP, Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025 and GenAI Security Project (accessed 2026-07-16). - OpenTelemetry, Generative AI semantic conventions (accessed 2026-07-16). Confirm convention stability before production adoption. docs.title: Risk-Aware Model Routing
docs.description: Route each request to the least costly qualified model without reducing required quality or control.
docs.text: Risk-Aware Model Routing Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Route each request to the least costly qualified model without reducing required quality or control. Why Static use of the largest model wastes cost; price-only routing creates safety regressions. When Use when task classes have stable, measurable requirements. How 1. Classify task, risk, data boundary, latency objective, and required capabilities. 2. Qualify candidate models per route on locked evaluations. 3. Apply deterministic policy before probabilistic routing. 4. Record route reason and fallback. 5. Requalify on provider/model changes and roll back a route on guardrail breach. Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Per-route qualification - Routing decision trace - Quality/cost frontier - Fallback test Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Enterprise considerations - Contract and residency are route constraints. - Maintain provider exit path. docs.title: Token Budget Standard
docs.description: Enforce per-task input, output, retry, and monthly token budgets.
docs.text: Token Budget Standard Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Enforce per-task input, output, retry, and monthly token budgets. Why Unbounded context and retries create denial-of-wallet and latency risk. When Use for every production model route. How 1. Set budgets from measured task distributions and SLOs. 2. Reserve tokens for safety instructions and structured output. 3. Trim by deterministic priority; never silently remove mandatory evidence. 4. Cap retries and total agent-loop spend. 5. Alert on forecast variance and degrade safely before hard exhaustion. Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Budget configuration - Truncation tests - Spend forecast - Override log Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Tradeoffs Choice Benefit Cost --- --- --- Hard cap Predictable spend Possible incomplete output Soft cap Flexible Runaway risk Anti-patterns - One global token limit. - Retrying malformed output indefinitely. Enterprise considerations - Budget by tenant and use case. - Require approval for temporary increases. docs.title: Continuous Evaluation
docs.description: Detect quality drift between releases and close the production-to-test feedback loop.
docs.text: Continuous Evaluation Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Detect quality drift between releases and close the production-to-test feedback loop. Why Provider behavior, traffic, knowledge, and adversaries change without repository changes. When Run on each change, scheduled canaries, sampled production traffic, and after incidents. How 1. Gate pull requests on deterministic and compact regression suites. 2. Run full suites nightly and on provider/model notices. 3. Sample production by risk and failure signals; redact before review. 4. Compare to a declared baseline with uncertainty and minimum sample size. 5. Freeze rollout, roll back, or degrade safely when guardrails breach; open and learn from an incident. Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - CI result with baseline delta - Scheduled run history - Sampling specification - Drift alert and response record Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Tradeoffs Choice Benefit Cost --- --- --- Frequent evaluation Fast detection Cost and reviewer load Sparse evaluation Lower cost Longer unsafe exposure Anti-patterns - Testing only when prompts change. - Alerting on noisy point estimates. - Reusing production data without authorization. Enterprise considerations - Use risk-weighted sampling. - Route telemetry through approved regions and processors. docs.title: Evaluation Framework Selection
docs.description: Define a qualified evaluation stack instead of selecting tools by popularity.
docs.text: Evaluation Framework Selection Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Define a qualified evaluation stack instead of selecting tools by popularity. Why Different evaluators expose different failure modes; no single score establishes fitness. When Use during platform selection and provider requalification. How 1. Inventory deterministic, reference-based, model-graded, security, latency, and cost checks. 2. Run a time-boxed bake-off on the same versioned golden set. 3. Measure agreement with blinded human labels, failure-detection rate, latency, cost, exportability, and data handling. 4. Select DeepEval for code-native gates, RAGAS for retrieval diagnostics, Promptfoo for adversarial matrices, and OpenTelemetry-compatible tracing for portable evidence. 5. Pin versions and requalify on material upgrades. Qualified tool roles Tool Normative role Release use Do not use as --- --- --- --- DeepEval Code-native test orchestration and regression assertions Pull-request and scheduled gates Sole RAG retrieval diagnosis RAGAS Retrieval and generation diagnostics for RAG pipelines Pre-release comparison and production sampling Sole security gate Promptfoo Provider/prompt matrices and adversarial testing Security campaigns and cross-provider qualification Sole proof of business correctness Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Bake-off report - Human/evaluator agreement with confidence intervals - False-pass and false-fail analysis - Data-flow and retention review Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. docs.text: Evaluation Metrics Catalog Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Define claim-level faithfulness, groundedness, context recall, hallucination rate, and decision rules. Why Metric names are often inconsistent; operational definitions prevent score laundering. When Use when specifying evaluation plans and dashboards. How 1. Faithfulness: supported claims divided by verifiable claims in supplied context. 2. Groundedness: weighted support score for each externally checkable claim against approved sources. 3. Context recall: required reference facts retrieved divided by all required facts. 4. Hallucination rate: unsupported or contradicted claims divided by verifiable claims; also report severe-case rate. 5. Report numerator, denominator, abstentions, confidence interval, slice results, judge version, and threshold rationale. docs.title: Prompt Versioning
docs.description: Treat prompts, schemas, tools, policies, and model settings as one immutable release unit.
docs.text: Prompt Versioning Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Treat prompts, schemas, tools, policies, and model settings as one immutable release unit. Why Prompt behavior depends on the entire execution envelope. When Use for every production prompt. How 1. Assign content-addressed versions. 2. Store source, variables, output schema, model settings, tool contracts, and owners. 3. Sign releases and preserve lineage. 4. Promote aliases only after gates pass. 5. Roll back aliases atomically. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. docs.description: Assess architecture fitness, risks, reversibility, and operational controls.
docs.text: Architecture Review Prompt Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 SDLC stage: 8 — Architecture Status: Explicit prompt template Purpose Assess architecture fitness, risks, reversibility, and operational controls. Why This prompt creates a reviewable artifact with explicit evidence, ownership, risk, and rollback instead of accepting fluent model output as proof. When Run at stage 8 — Architecture. Re-run whenever requirements, dependencies, model/provider versions, risk classification, or production evidence changes. How 1. Supply authoritative source material and identify unknowns. 2. Execute the prompt without granting unreviewed side effects. 3. Verify every cited fact and command against the repository or system of record. 4. Record the reviewer, decision, evidence links, and rollback trigger. Tradeoffs Benefit Cost --- --- Repeatable, auditable output Input preparation and review time Explicit stop conditions Less apparent autonomy Anti-patterns - Treating generated text as approval or objective evidence. - Omitting rollback because a change appears small. - Allowing the authoring agent to be the sole approver for high-risk work. Enterprise considerations - Retain prompt version, inputs, outputs, model/provider identity, evidence, and decision under the applicable retention policy. - Apply least privilege and redact restricted data before model submission. - Requalify after provider, model, policy, or material prompt changes. Checklist - [ ] Inputs are authoritative and complete. - [ ] Output cites objective evidence. - [ ] Named human approval is captured where required. - [ ] Rollback and incident-loop actions are executable. - [ ] Unknowns and residual risk are explicit. References - NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and Generative AI Profile (accessed 2026-07-16). - ISO, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and ISO/IEC 23894:2023 (accessed 2026-07-16). docs.title: Agent Quality Standard
docs.description: Require bounded authority, observable state, termination, recovery, and human control for agents.
docs.text: Agent Quality Standard Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Require bounded authority, observable state, termination, recovery, and human control for agents. Why Autonomous loops amplify small errors into repeated side effects. When Apply to any system that selects tools or acts over multiple steps. How 1. Define role, allowed tools, memory scope, communication protocol, and prohibited actions. 2. Enforce least privilege outside the model. 3. Set step, time, token, cost, and side-effect budgets. 4. Require idempotency, checkpoints, and compensating actions. 5. Test failure, interruption, tool deception, and human handoff. Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Policy tests - Tool authorization logs - Termination tests - Recovery drill Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Tradeoffs Choice Benefit Cost --- --- --- Bounded agent Safer and diagnosable Reduced autonomy Anti-patterns - Giving broad credentials to improve completion. - Using model refusal as the only guardrail. Enterprise considerations - Segregate duties for high-impact actions. - Log proposed, approved, and executed actions.
