docs.title: Level 8: AI SDLC
docs.description: Preserve the complete 26-stage v1.0 lifecycle while applying a mandatory baseline and risk-based control depth.
docs.text: Level 8: AI SDLC Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Preserve the complete 26-stage v1.0 lifecycle while applying a mandatory baseline and risk-based control depth. Why A rigid 26-stage ceremony wastes low-risk effort, while stage skipping removes evidence. Tailoring changes depth, independence, and cadence—not accountability. When Use for every software or AI change. How 1. Run the baseline: intake and outcome; testable requirements; risk classification; plan; implementation; review; verification; controlled release; monitoring; learning and closure. 2. Map the baseline to the original stages: 1–6 intake/context, 7–10 plan/approve, 11–13 build/review, 14–19 verify/document, 20–22 release/operate, 23–26 learn/close. 3. Low risk may combine artifacts and use peer approval. Medium risk requires independent security/evaluation review and canary. High risk requires domain, security/privacy/risk approvals, human oversight, red team, rollback drill, and enhanced monitoring. 4. Never remove stages 9 human accountability, 14 verification, 16 security disposition, 20 controlled release, 21 monitoring, or 23–25 incident learning; record not-applicable decisions with rationale. 5. Use the prompt and quality-standard catalogs below. v1.0 stage map Stage Original scope Baseline workstream Required evidence --- --- --- --- 1 Idea Intake and outcome Problem and outcome statement 2 Research Intake and outcome Source and feasibility evidence 3 Requirements Requirements and risk Testable requirements 4 Story kickoff Requirements and risk Approved story 5 Context collection Requirements and risk Context inventory and provenance 6 Knowledge gathering Requirements and risk Assumptions and knowledge gaps 7 Planning Plan and approve Implementation plan 8 Architecture Plan and approve Architecture decision and threat model 9 Human approval Plan and approve Named decision, date, and conditions 10 Prompt generation Plan and approve Versioned prompt artifact and tests 11 Coding Build and review Reviewable change set 12 Self review Build and review Author checklist and test evidence 13 Agent review Build and review Independent automated findings with human disposition 14 Testing Verify and document Deterministic test report 15 Evaluation Verify and document Versioned evaluation report 16 Security Verify and document Security findings and disposition 17 Performance Verify and document Baseline comparison and capacity evidence 18 Accessibility Verify and document Accessibility verification 19 Documentation Verify and document User, operator, API, and decision updates 20 Deployment Release and operate Go/no-go, canary, and rollback record 21 Monitoring Release and operate SLO, trace, dashboard, and alert validation 22 Continuous improvement Release and operate Production-review and backlog loop 23 Postmortem Learn and close Incident analysis when triggered; otherwise release review 24 Lessons learned Learn and close Verified lessons and action owners 25 Knowledge base update Learn and close Searchable decisions, runbooks, and regression cases 26 Feature complete Learn and close Definition-of-Done approval Risk-based tailoring Risk Permitted tailoring Mandatory depth --- --- --- Low Combine related stage artifacts; peer approval; sampled post-release review Baseline criteria, security disposition, tests, rollback, monitoring, and closure evidence Medium Combine only intake or documentation artifacts Independent security/evaluation review, canary, explicit human release approval, and incident drill High No combined decision gates Domain, security, privacy, and risk approval; red team; human action oversight; rollback exercise; enhanced monitoring and appeal Prompt catalog - Story Kickoff - Implementation Plan - Architecture Review - Coding - Refactoring - Security Review - Performance Review - Test Generation - Documentation - Release - Incident - Root Cause Analysis - Migration - Technical Debt - Knowledge Capture Quality standards - Definition of Ready - Definition of Done - Prompt Quality - Agent Quality - Code Quality Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Risk classification - Stage-tailoring record - Approval and gate evidence - Release/rollback record - Knowledge update Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Tradeoffs Choice Benefit Cost --- --- --- Risk tailoring Proportional effort Classification governance Uniform depth Simple Waste or insufficient control Anti-patterns - Calling tailoring stage skipping. - Classifying risk after implementation. Enterprise considerations - High-risk decisions retain genuine human review and appeal. - Tailoring records are retained with the release evidence and reviewed by the accountable owner. - Provider or model changes trigger evaluation and provider requalification before promotion. Control mapping Source Practical mapping Claim boundary --- --- --- NIST AI RMF Govern, Map, Measure, and Manage evidence Alignment aid; not NIST approval ISO/IEC 42001 and 23894 Management-system and AI-risk control inputs No certification is asserted OWASP GenAI Threat scenarios and verification cases Coverage does not prove security Checklist - [ ] All 26 stages are mapped. - [ ] Tailoring rationale approved. - [ ] Incident loop is operational. References - NIST, AI Risk Management Framework 1.0 and Generative AI Profile (accessed 2026-07-16). - ISO, ISO/IEC 42001:2023 and ISO/IEC 23894:2023 (accessed 2026-07-16). docs.text: Provider-Neutral AI Harness Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Decouple applications from provider SDKs while preserving provider-specific safety and capability controls. Why A stable contract enables failover and requalification; a lowest-common-denominator wrapper hides critical differences. When Use for enterprise applications calling external or self-hosted models. How 1. Define canonical request, response, error, usage, tool, and policy contracts. 2. Implement adapters that expose declared capability differences. 3. Centralize identity, data policy, redaction, tracing, budgets, and evaluation hooks. 4. Qualify every provider/route independently. 5. Test exit, export, failover, and rollback at least annually. Objective evidence Retain evidence with artifact version, source revision, model and provider identifiers, dataset version, evaluator version, timestamp, owner, and approval decision. - Contract tests - Capability matrix - Failover game day - Provider requalification Rollback and incident loop Define a tested rollback trigger before release. On breach, stop or constrain the affected capability, restore the last qualified artifact, preserve traces, notify the accountable human, and open an incident. Convert confirmed failures into regression cases; close the incident only after remediation passes the same gate and the runbook is updated. Human oversight A named human owns the decision. Automation may recommend or block, but it must not silently waive a failed control. High-impact actions require review before execution; emergency overrides are time-bound, logged, and reviewed after use. Tradeoffs Choice Benefit Cost --- --- --- Neutral harness Portability and control Adapter maintenance Anti-patterns - Leaking provider objects into application code. - Failing over without data-boundary checks. docs.text: OAuth 2.1 for MCP Servers Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Secure MCP access with standards-based delegated authorization and resource-bound tokens. docs.text: Agent Tool Sandboxing Version: 1.0.0 Last updated: 2026-07-16 Status: OAIES normative guidance Purpose Isolate code and tool execution from hosts, networks, credentials, and tenants. Why Generated commands and dependencies are untrusted workloads. When Use for code execution, browsing, file processing, and extensible tools. How 1. Use ephemeral non-root workloads with read-only base images. 2. Deny network by default and allowlist destinations. 3. Mount only required files and inject short-lived scoped credentials. 4. docs.title: OAIES Quality Checklists
docs.description: Checklists are not suggestions. They are gates. A stage is not complete until its checklist passes.
docs.text: OAIES Quality Checklists Gate every stage. Skip none. These checklists are the standard. --- How to Use Checklists Checklists are not suggestions. They are gates. A stage is not complete until its checklist passes. Rule: If you cannot check an item, stop. Either fix the issue or explicitly document why the item does not apply (with a named approver). --- Checklist Index Checklist When to Use ----------- ------------ Planning Checklist Before implementation begins Coding Checklist Before submitting for review Review Checklist During code/prompt review Security Checklist Before deployment Deployment Checklist Before releasing Prompt Checklist Before using a prompt in production Agent Checklist Before deploying an agent Context Checklist Before assembling model context Performance Checklist Before performance sign-off Architecture Checklist Before architectural decisions --- Planning Checklist Gate: No coding until all planning items pass. Story Quality - [ ] Story has clear "As a [user], I want [action], so that [benefit]" format - [ ] Acceptance criteria are testable (a QA engineer can write tests from them) - [ ] At least 3 acceptance criteria (happy path + 2 edge cases) - [ ] Out-of-scope items explicitly listed - [ ] Dependencies identified and available Technical Planning - [ ] Implementation plan reviewed and approved (named approver + date) - [ ] All files to be changed listed by path - [ ] Data model changes identified (schema, migration, backward compatibility) - [ ] API contract changes identified (breaking vs. non-breaking) - [ ] Rollback strategy defined - [ ] Estimated effort matches story size Risk Assessment - [ ] Top 3 risks identified with mitigations - [ ] Security risk considered (even for non-security features) - [ ] Performance impact estimated - [ ] External dependencies confirmed available --- Coding Checklist Gate: Self-review before requesting peer review. Correctness - [ ] Implementation matches acceptance criteria (verify each one) - [ ] Edge cases from story are handled - [ ] Error handling is complete (every error path handled, not just happy path) - [ ] Null/undefined/empty checks present where needed - [ ] No hardcoded values that should be configurable Code Quality - [ ] No code duplication that should be extracted - [ ] Functions do one thing (single responsibility) - [ ] Variable and function names are self-documenting - [ ] Complex logic has comments explaining WHY (not WHAT) - [ ] No dead code or commented-out code committed Testing - [ ] Unit tests for all new logic - [ ] Tests cover happy path, error path, and edge cases - [ ] Tests are independent (no test depends on another) - [ ] No assertions against implementation details (test behavior) - [ ] Coverage percentage not reduced Type Safety (TypeScript/Python) - [ ] No any types (TypeScript) or untyped functions (Python) - [ ] Null cases handled explicitly - [ ] Return types explicit on all public functions --- Security Checklist Gate: Must pass before deployment to production. Input Validation - [ ] All user inputs validated for type, length, and allowed characters - [ ] Prompt injection patterns checked if user input reaches AI context - [ ] File uploads validated for type and size - [ ] URL inputs validated against allowlist if used for outbound requests Authorization - [ ] All protected routes/resources check authorization - [ ] Horizontal privilege escalation tested (user A cannot access user B's data) - [ ] Vertical privilege escalation tested (user cannot access admin functions) Data Protection - [ ] No secrets in source code (use environment variables or secret manager) - [ ] Sensitive data not logged (passwords, tokens, PII, payment data) - [ ] PII encrypted at rest and in transit - [ ] Database queries use parameterized statements (no string interpolation) AI-Specific - [ ] User input separated from system instructions in prompts - [ ] Tool execution respects user permissions (not just model instructions) - [ ] Multi-tenant context isolation verified at database level - [ ] Model output validated before acting on it --- Prompt Checklist Gate: No prompt deployed to production without passing this checklist. Structure - [ ] Uses XML structure standard (role, context, instructions, outputformat, constraints) - [ ] Role definition is specific with explicit exclusions - [ ] Context is complete and noise-free (no irrelevant information) - [ ] Instructions are numbered and imperative - [ ] Output format is explicit with a concrete example Quality - [ ] At least 3 hard constraints - [ ] Planning/thinking step included for complex tasks - [ ] No implicit assumptions (everything is explicit) - [ ] Tested with at least 5 inputs including 2 adversarial ones Operations - [ ] Prompt is versioned in registry (Langfuse/PromptLayer/Braintrust) - [ ] Evaluation test cases exist and pass - [ ] Changelog entry written for this version - [ ] Rollback version identified --- Agent Checklist Gate: No agent deployed without passing this checklist. Definition - [ ] Role is specific with explicit exclusions - [ ] Tools list matches minimum needed (no over-permissioning) - [ ] Memory requirements documented - [ ] Communication protocol defined (who it receives from, who it sends to) Reliability - [ ] Success termination criteria defined - [ ] Failure termination criteria defined (including max iterations) - [ ] Retry strategy specified - [ ] Recovery strategy for each major failure mode Safety - [ ] Tool execution requires harness validation - [ ] High-impact operations require human approval - [ ] Agent cannot exceed user's permissions - [ ] All agent actions are audited Testing - [ ] Tested with 10+ end-to-end scenarios - [ ] Adversarial inputs tested (prompt injection, unusual edge cases) - [ ] Failure recovery tested (what happens when a tool fails?) - [ ] Loop detection verified (agent cannot run infinitely) --- Deployment Checklist Gate: No deployment to production without passing this checklist. Pre-Deployment - [ ] All automated tests passing (unit, integration, evaluation) - [ ] Security review completed and signed off - [ ] Performance review completed (no regression) - [ ] Documentation updated - [ ] CHANGELOG updated with this release - [ ] Rollback plan documented and tested Deployment Execution - [ ] Deploy to staging first - [ ] Smoke tests passing in staging - [ ] Monitoring dashboards ready - [ ] On-call engineer notified/available Post-Deployment - [ ] Smoke tests passing in production - [ ] Error rate baseline confirmed (no unexpected increase) - [ ] Latency baseline confirmed - [ ] Cost metrics confirmed (no unexpected spike) - [ ] Deployment marked stable (or rollback initiated within 15 minutes) --- Architecture Checklist Gate: No architectural change without passing this checklist. - [ ] ADR created for this decision - [ ] At least 3 options considered (documented in ADR) - [ ] Decision drivers explicitly listed and ranked - [ ] Tradeoffs documented for chosen option - [ ] Consequences (positive and negative) documented - [ ] Security implications reviewed - [ ] Performance implications estimated - [ ] Compliance implications reviewed (if enterprise) - [ ] Reversibility assessed (can this be undone if wrong?) - [ ] ADR reviewed by at least one peer - [ ] ADR status set to ACCEPTED by named approver

docs.title: Contributing to OAIES
docs.description: This repository defines a standard. Contributions that lower that standard are rejected — respectfully, but firmly.
docs.text: Contributing to OAIES The Standard for Contributing This repository defines a standard. Contributions that lower that standard are rejected — respectfully, but firmly. Before opening a PR, ask yourself: Would a principal engineer at Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft, or Google approve this? --- What We Accept ✅ High-value contributions - New AI Engineering Patterns (full 13-component specification required) - New cookbook entries for unlisted technology stacks - Updates to existing content based on production learnings - New MCP integration specs - Anti-pattern additions with root cause analysis - Corrections to factual errors with citations ❌ We do not accept - "Awesome lists" of tools without integration guidance - Tutorial-style content ("Let me explain what an LLM is...") - Hedged recommendations ("You could do X or Y or Z...") - Unverified claims without production evidence - Placeholder content or TODOs - Generic advice that applies to any software project --- Document Quality Standard Every contribution MUST include: Required Element Description --- --- Purpose One sentence — what problem this solves Why The reasoning — why this approach over alternatives Tradeoffs What you give up by choosing this approach Anti-pattern At least one thing NOT to do, with root cause Enterprise note Compliance, scale, or governance consideration Checklist Minimum verifiable quality gates (at least 3 items) Missing any of these = PR closed. --- File Naming Conventions Follow these exactly. PRs that deviate will be asked to rename. --- Adding a New AI Engineering Pattern Patterns are the most valuable contribution. Each must contain all 13 components: --- PR Checklist Before submitting: - [ ] All required document elements present - [ ] File naming follows conventions - [ ] No placeholder text or TODOs - [ ] Mermaid diagrams render correctly - [ ] All internal links are valid - [ ] Content is written at principal-engineer level - [ ] Enterprise considerations documented - [ ] Anti-patterns included - [ ] Changelog updated --- Code of Conduct We hold content to a high standard — not contributors. Everyone is welcome regardless of experience level. The bar is on the contribution, not the contributor. If your PR is rejected, the feedback will be specific and constructive. Use it to improve the contribution and resubmit. --- OAIES — "The standard doesn't tell you what you can do. It tells you what you must do."

docs.title: Accessibility Engineering Architecture Patterns
docs.description: Define the default production architecture for a Accessibility Engineering workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve.
docs.text: Accessibility Engineering Architecture Patterns Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define the default production architecture for a Accessibility Engineering workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve. Why Start with native semantics, make every operation keyboard-complete, test with assistive technology, and treat automated scans as a floor. A stable boundary reduces coupling, limits failure propagation, and makes ownership auditable. How Use Accessible primitive layer: Design-system primitives encode semantics, focus, contrast, and input behavior; product flows test composition. Boundary rules 1. Validate identity, authorization, and input before domain mutation. 2. Keep dependency-specific types behind the infrastructure port. 3. Attach deadlines, cancellation, idempotency, and retry classification at the call boundary. 4. Emit traceable outcomes without secret or regulated payload leakage. 5. Version contracts and migrate producers before removing compatibility. Tradeoffs The extra adapter and contract code costs initial delivery time. It buys isolated tests, replaceable infrastructure, clearer ownership, and safer migrations. Anti-patterns - Patch inaccessible custom widgets with arbitrary ARIA. This couples unrelated change rates and expands blast radius. - Do not hide remote calls, unbounded work, or mutable global state behind convenience helpers. - Do not introduce a distributed boundary without an owner, SLO, timeout, and failure policy. Enterprise considerations Assign owners to every boundary and data class. Enforce policy as code, retain architecture decisions and deployment evidence, and design regional, tenant, and regulatory isolation before data is written. Official guidance - WCAG 2.2 - WAI-ARIA APG - ARIA specification Checklist - [ ] Domain and infrastructure boundaries are visible in code and telemetry. - [ ] Trust, data, transaction, and rollback boundaries are documented. - [ ] Dependency failure is bounded and tested. - [ ] Contract evolution is backward compatible. - [ ] Ownership and SLO are assigned. Changelog - 1.0.0 (2026-07-16): Added production architecture pattern.

docs.title: Accessibility Engineering Code Review Checklist
docs.description: Review a Accessibility Engineering change for correctness, security, operability, and maintainability before merge.
docs.text: Accessibility Engineering Code Review Checklist Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Review a Accessibility Engineering change for correctness, security, operability, and maintainability before merge. Why Checklists convert production expectations into auditable yes/no gates and prevent AI-generated plausibility from replacing runtime evidence. How Review the diff with repository context, then execute validators. Record only evidence-backed findings with a required fix and verification method. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated accessible component, user flow, audit, remediation plan, or conformance gate without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - WCAG 2.2 - WAI-ARIA APG - ARIA specification Checklist - [ ] Change follows the governing stance: Start with native semantics, make every operation keyboard-complete, test with assistive technology, and treat automated scans as a floor. - [ ] Public behavior and compatibility impact are documented. - [ ] Input validation, authorization, output encoding, and secret handling match the threat model. - [ ] Failure paths define timeout, cancellation, retry safety, idempotency, and cleanup where applicable. - [ ] Concurrency and transaction behavior preserve data invariants. - [ ] Logs, metrics, and traces identify outcomes without sensitive payloads. - [ ] Tests cover success, boundary, failure, and recovery behavior. - [ ] Native formatter, static analysis, tests, security checks, and build pass. - [ ] Native semantics are used first. - [ ] Keyboard path and focus are deterministic. - [ ] Name/role/value are exposed. - [ ] Manual assistive-technology tests pass. - [ ] Documentation and runbooks match changed behavior. docs.title: Accessibility Engineering Common Error Workflow
docs.description: Diagnose recurring Accessibility Engineering failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error.
docs.text: Accessibility Engineering Common Error Workflow Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Diagnose recurring Accessibility Engineering failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error. Why Error text is a symptom, not a root cause. This workflow requires a discriminating observation before each repair. How 1. Preserve timestamps, correlation identifiers, artifact version, topology, and recent changes. 2. Stabilize user impact with the smallest reversible mitigation. 3. Capture the evidence named below before restarting or clearing state. 4. Test one ranked hypothesis at a time. 5. Add a regression test, alert, or policy after confirming root cause. Symptom Likely causal class Required repair Primary evidence --- --- --- --- Interactive control has no accessible name Visible styling is not programmatically associated with the control. Use native label association or an accurate aria-labelledby relationship. accessibility tree Keyboard focus is trapped or lost Focus management ignores open/close, route, or disabled-state transitions. Define entry, cycle, escape, and return-focus behavior. keyboard-only test ARIA state differs from visual state Custom widget does not update its semantic state. Prefer native control or update state atomically with UI behavior. screen reader and accessibility tree Insufficient color contrast Foreground/background combination fails the required contrast criterion. Change design tokens and test all states, including focus and disabled. contrast analyzer Dynamic update is not announced Important asynchronous content lacks suitable status semantics or focus strategy. Use restrained live regions or move focus when context truly changes. screen-reader test 1. Interactive control has no accessible name Confirm: Capture accessibility tree and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Visible styling is not programmatically associated with the control. Repair: Use native label association or an accurate aria-labelledby relationship. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 2. Keyboard focus is trapped or lost Confirm: Capture keyboard-only test and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Focus management ignores open/close, route, or disabled-state transitions. Repair: Define entry, cycle, escape, and return-focus behavior. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 3. ARIA state differs from visual state Confirm: Capture screen reader and accessibility tree and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Custom widget does not update its semantic state. Repair: Prefer native control or update state atomically with UI behavior. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 4. Insufficient color contrast Confirm: Capture contrast analyzer and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Foreground/background combination fails the required contrast criterion. Repair: Change design tokens and test all states, including focus and disabled. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 5. Dynamic update is not announced Confirm: Capture screen-reader test and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Important asynchronous content lacks suitable status semantics or focus strategy. Repair: Use restrained live regions or move focus when context truly changes. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated diagnostic or repair without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - WCAG 2.2 - WAI-ARIA APG - ARIA specification Checklist - [ ] Incident timeline and affected artifact identity are preserved. - [ ] Root cause explains every material observation. - [ ] Mitigation is reversible and does not destroy forensic state. - [ ] Permanent fix has a regression test. - [ ] Recovery is confirmed through user-impact telemetry. Changelog - 1.0.0 (2026-07-16): Added production five-error diagnostic workflow.

docs.text: Accessibility Engineering Cookbook Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose This cookbook turns Accessibility Engineering production guidance into reusable prompts, a procedural skill, diagnostics, architecture patterns, and release gates. Why AI output is safe only when constrained by the runtime's real contracts. For Accessibility Engineering, the decisive concerns are WCAG conformance, semantic UI, keyboard operation, focus, assistive technology testing, and governance. The governing stance is: Start with native semantics, make every operation keyboard-complete, test with assistive technology, and treat automated scans as a floor. When to use Use this cookbook to generate, review, debug, or deploy a accessible component, user flow, audit, remediation plan, or conformance gate. Do not use it as a substitute for repository conventions, threat modeling, load testing, or operator approval. How 1. Start with prompts/generate.prompt.md and supply repository evidence. 2. Run native format, static-analysis, test, security, and build commands. 3. Apply prompts/review.prompt.md; block on unresolved correctness or security findings. 4. Use debug-workflows/common-errors.md from observed evidence, not guesses. 5. Enforce both files under checklists/ before release. Contents - Three production XML prompts: generate, review, and debug. - One trigger-based accessibility.skill.md. - Five evidence-led common-error workflows. - One opinionated architecture pattern. - Separate code-review and deployment gates. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated accessible component, user flow, audit, remediation plan, or conformance gate without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - WCAG 2.2 - WAI-ARIA APG - ARIA specification Checklist - [ ] Native semantics are used first. - [ ] Keyboard path and focus are deterministic. - [ ] Name/role/value are exposed. - [ ] Manual assistive-technology tests pass. - [ ] Links in this cookbook resolve to official guidance. - [ ] Prompt output includes no unresolved variables. docs.description: Provide a deterministic procedure for generating, changing, diagnosing, or releasing a accessible component, user flow, audit, remediation plan, or conformance
docs.text: Accessibility Engineering Production Skill Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Provide a deterministic procedure for generating, changing, diagnosing, or releasing a accessible component, user flow, audit, remediation plan, or conformance gate with AI assistance. Trigger Activate when a request changes Accessibility Engineering source, configuration, infrastructure, data contracts, or production behavior. Do not activate for a documentation-only mention with no technical decision. Why Start with native semantics, make every operation keyboard-complete, test with assistive technology, and treat automated scans as a floor. The skill converts that principle into evidence gates that an agent cannot skip. Inputs - Repository rules and ownership boundaries. - Exact runtime/toolchain evidence from manifests or platform APIs. - Requested behavior and acceptance tests. - Sanitized logs, traces, metrics, plans, or screenshots when diagnosing. - Deployment topology, SLO, data classification, and rollback mechanism. How 1. Discover the nearest repository instructions and established implementation pattern. 2. State the invariant, trust boundary, failure mode, and rollback boundary. 3. Select the matching prompt under ../prompts/. 4. Make the smallest coherent change; preserve public contracts unless migration is approved. 5. Run native formatting, static analysis, unit/integration tests, security checks, and build/package validation. 6. Apply ../checklists/code-review.md. 7. For release work, apply ../checklists/deployment.md and capture evidence. Verification 1. Verify that native semantics are used first. 2. Verify that keyboard path and focus are deterministic. 3. Verify that name/role/value are exposed. 4. Verify that manual assistive-technology tests pass. 5. Record commands, exit status, artifact identity, and links to retained evidence. Unhappy path and recovery - If repository or version evidence is missing, stop and request it. - If a validator fails, fix the first causal error; never suppress the rule as the initial response. - If the failure cannot be reproduced, improve telemetry and preserve the incident state. - If a release gate fails, halt progression and execute the documented rollback or feature-disable path. - If credentials or regulated data appear in context, stop, revoke or rotate as required, and follow incident policy. Communication protocol Report decisions, changed files, commands actually run, observed results, residual risks, and an explicit ship/block recommendation. Distinguish facts from hypotheses. Termination criteria Finish only when acceptance tests and both relevant checklists pass, or when a named blocker with owner and required evidence is recorded. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated accessible component, user flow, audit, remediation plan, or conformance gate without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - WCAG 2.2 - WAI-ARIA APG - ARIA specification Checklist - [ ] Trigger and scope are valid. - [ ] Inputs are complete and sanitized. - [ ] Native validators pass. - [ ] Failure and rollback paths are tested. - [ ] Evidence is retained under project policy. Why Checklists convert production expectations into auditable yes/no gates and prevent AI-generated plausibility from replacing runtime evidence. How Review the diff with repository context, then execute validators. Record only evidence-backed findings with a required fix and verification method. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational runbook without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - AWS Architecture Center - AWS Well-Architected - IAM best practices Checklist - [ ] Change follows the governing stance: Use short-lived role credentials, multi-account boundaries, infrastructure as code, and failure isolation designed from service quotas. - [ ] Public behavior and compatibility impact are documented. - [ ] Input validation, authorization, output encoding, and secret handling match the threat model. - [ ] Failure paths define timeout, cancellation, retry safety, idempotency, and cleanup where applicable. - [ ] Concurrency and transaction behavior preserve data invariants. - [ ] Logs, metrics, and traces identify outcomes without sensitive payloads. - [ ] Tests cover success, boundary, failure, and recovery behavior. - [ ] Native formatter, static analysis, tests, security checks, and build pass. - [ ] IAM policy is least privilege. - [ ] Network and account boundaries are explicit. - [ ] Alarms map to user impact. - [ ] Quotas and retry budgets are tested. - [ ] Documentation and runbooks match changed behavior. Changelog - 1.0.0 (2026-07-16): Added production code review checklist.

docs.text: AWS Deployment Checklist Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Block unsafe promotion of a AWS artifact and retain evidence for rollback and audit. Why Checklists convert production expectations into auditable yes/no gates and prevent AI-generated plausibility from replacing runtime evidence. How Execute in order before each environment promotion. A failed item blocks promotion; do not convert it to a warning without named risk acceptance. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational runbook without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - AWS Architecture Center - AWS Well-Architected - IAM best practices Checklist - [ ] Artifact is immutable, uniquely identified, scanned, and produced by the approved pipeline. - [ ] Configuration, schema, identity, policy, and dependency changes were reviewed together. - [ ] Backward compatibility is proven across the rollout window. - [ ] Secrets are referenced from the approved secret system and were not embedded in artifacts or logs. - [ ] Capacity, quotas, timeouts, retries, and concurrency limits match expected load. - [ ] Dashboards and alerts report user impact, saturation, errors, and dependency health. - [ ] Progressive rollout has explicit pause, success, and automatic rollback thresholds. - [ ] Rollback or feature-disable path was exercised against the release candidate. - [ ] Post-deployment smoke tests verify the critical path and negative authorization path. - [ ] Owner records artifact identity, approvals, results, and residual risk. docs.title: AWS Common Error Workflow
docs.description: Diagnose recurring AWS failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error.
docs.text: AWS Common Error Workflow Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Diagnose recurring AWS failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error. Why Error text is a symptom, not a root cause. This workflow requires a discriminating observation before each repair. How 1. Preserve timestamps, correlation identifiers, artifact version, topology, and recent changes. 2. Stabilize user impact with the smallest reversible mitigation. 3. Capture the evidence named below before restarting or clearing state. 4. Test one ranked hypothesis at a time. 5. Add a regression test, alert, or policy after confirming root cause. Symptom Likely causal class Required repair Primary evidence --- --- --- --- AccessDenied Identity policy, resource policy, boundary, SCP, or explicit deny blocks the action. Evaluate the full policy chain and narrow the required action/resource. CloudTrail and policy simulator CloudFormation UPDATEROLLBACKFAILED Rollback could not restore a dependent resource. Correct the resource cause, continue rollback, then redeploy a reviewed change set. stack events Lambda task timed out Work exceeds timeout due to dependency latency, cold start, or unbounded processing. Trace dependencies, bound work, and set timeout below caller budget. X-Ray and CloudWatch Logs ThrottlingException Concurrency or API rate exceeds a service quota. Honor backoff, add jitter, cap concurrency, and assess quota evidence. CloudWatch metrics VPC endpoint/DNS connectivity failure Routes, security groups, NACLs, endpoint policy, or DNS are inconsistent. Trace the exact source-destination path and policy layers. VPC Flow Logs 1. AccessDenied Confirm: Capture CloudTrail and policy simulator and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Identity policy, resource policy, boundary, SCP, or explicit deny blocks the action. Repair: Evaluate the full policy chain and narrow the required action/resource. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 2. CloudFormation UPDATEROLLBACKFAILED Confirm: Capture stack events and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Rollback could not restore a dependent resource. Repair: Correct the resource cause, continue rollback, then redeploy a reviewed change set. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 3. Lambda task timed out Confirm: Capture X-Ray and CloudWatch Logs and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Work exceeds timeout due to dependency latency, cold start, or unbounded processing. Repair: Trace dependencies, bound work, and set timeout below caller budget. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 4. ThrottlingException Confirm: Capture CloudWatch metrics and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Concurrency or API rate exceeds a service quota. Repair: Honor backoff, add jitter, cap concurrency, and assess quota evidence. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 5. VPC endpoint/DNS connectivity failure Confirm: Capture VPC Flow Logs and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Routes, security groups, NACLs, endpoint policy, or DNS are inconsistent. Repair: Trace the exact source-destination path and policy layers. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated diagnostic or repair without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - AWS Architecture Center - AWS Well-Architected - IAM best practices Checklist - [ ] Incident timeline and affected artifact identity are preserved. - [ ] Root cause explains every material observation. - [ ] Mitigation is reversible and does not destroy forensic state. - [ ] Permanent fix has a regression test. - [ ] Recovery is confirmed through user-impact telemetry. Changelog - 1.0.0 (2026-07-16): Added production five-error diagnostic workflow.

docs.description: This cookbook turns AWS production guidance into reusable prompts, a procedural skill, diagnostics, architecture patterns, and release gates.
docs.text: AWS Cookbook Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose This cookbook turns AWS production guidance into reusable prompts, a procedural skill, diagnostics, architecture patterns, and release gates. Why AI output is safe only when constrained by the runtime's real contracts. For AWS, the decisive concerns are IAM, networking, managed services, infrastructure as code, reliability, observability, and cost controls. The governing stance is: Use short-lived role credentials, multi-account boundaries, infrastructure as code, and failure isolation designed from service quotas. When to use Use this cookbook to generate, review, debug, or deploy a AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational runbook. Do not use it as a substitute for repository conventions, threat modeling, load testing, or operator approval. How 1. Start with prompts/generate.prompt.md and supply repository evidence. 2. Run native format, static-analysis, test, security, and build commands. 3. Apply prompts/review.prompt.md; block on unresolved correctness or security findings. 4. Use debug-workflows/common-errors.md from observed evidence, not guesses. 5. Enforce both files under checklists/ before release. Contents - Three production XML prompts: generate, review, and debug. - One trigger-based aws.skill.md. - Five evidence-led common-error workflows. - One opinionated architecture pattern. - Separate code-review and deployment gates. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational runbook without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - AWS Architecture Center - AWS Well-Architected - IAM best practices Checklist - [ ] IAM policy is least privilege. - [ ] Network and account boundaries are explicit. - [ ] Alarms map to user impact. - [ ] Quotas and retry budgets are tested. - [ ] Links in this cookbook resolve to official guidance. - [ ] Prompt output includes no unresolved variables. docs.title: AWS Production Skill
docs.description: Provide a deterministic procedure for generating, changing, diagnosing, or releasing a AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational r
docs.text: AWS Production Skill Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Provide a deterministic procedure for generating, changing, diagnosing, or releasing a AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational runbook with AI assistance. Trigger Activate when a request changes AWS source, configuration, infrastructure, data contracts, or production behavior. Do not activate for a documentation-only mention with no technical decision. Why Use short-lived role credentials, multi-account boundaries, infrastructure as code, and failure isolation designed from service quotas. The skill converts that principle into evidence gates that an agent cannot skip. Inputs - Repository rules and ownership boundaries. - Exact runtime/toolchain evidence from manifests or platform APIs. - Requested behavior and acceptance tests. - Sanitized logs, traces, metrics, plans, or screenshots when diagnosing. - Deployment topology, SLO, data classification, and rollback mechanism. How 1. Discover the nearest repository instructions and established implementation pattern. 2. State the invariant, trust boundary, failure mode, and rollback boundary. 3. Select the matching prompt under ../prompts/. 4. Make the smallest coherent change; preserve public contracts unless migration is approved. 5. Run native formatting, static analysis, unit/integration tests, security checks, and build/package validation. 6. Apply ../checklists/code-review.md. 7. For release work, apply ../checklists/deployment.md and capture evidence. Verification 1. Verify that IAM policy is least privilege. 2. Verify that network and account boundaries are explicit. 3. Verify that alarms map to user impact. 4. Verify that quotas and retry budgets are tested. 5. Record commands, exit status, artifact identity, and links to retained evidence. Unhappy path and recovery - If repository or version evidence is missing, stop and request it. - If a validator fails, fix the first causal error; never suppress the rule as the initial response. - If the failure cannot be reproduced, improve telemetry and preserve the incident state. - If a release gate fails, halt progression and execute the documented rollback or feature-disable path. - If credentials or regulated data appear in context, stop, revoke or rotate as required, and follow incident policy. Communication protocol Report decisions, changed files, commands actually run, observed results, residual risks, and an explicit ship/block recommendation. Distinguish facts from hypotheses. Termination criteria Finish only when acceptance tests and both relevant checklists pass, or when a named blocker with owner and required evidence is recorded. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated AWS workload, CloudFormation/CDK stack, Lambda function, or operational runbook without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - AWS Architecture Center - AWS Well-Architected - IAM best practices Checklist - [ ] Trigger and scope are valid. - [ ] Inputs are complete and sanitized. - [ ] Native validators pass. - [ ] Failure and rollback paths are tested. - [ ] Evidence is retained under project policy. Changelog - 1.0.0 (2026-07-16): Added production skill.

docs.title: Azure Architecture Patterns
docs.description: Define the default production architecture for a Azure workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve.
docs.text: Azure Architecture Patterns Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define the default production architecture for a Azure workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve. Why Prefer managed identity, private connectivity, declarative infrastructure, policy enforcement, and measurable reliability targets. A stable boundary reduces coupling, limits failure propagation, and makes ownership auditable. How Use Landing-zone workload slice: Subscriptions, identity, network, policy, observability, and workload resources are independently governed modules. Boundary rules 1. Validate identity, authorization, and input before domain mutation. 2. Keep dependency-specific types behind the infrastructure port. 3. Attach deadlines, cancellation, idempotency, and retry classification at the call boundary. 4. Emit traceable outcomes without secret or regulated payload leakage. 5. Version contracts and migrate producers before removing compatibility. Tradeoffs The extra adapter and contract code costs initial delivery time. It buys isolated tests, replaceable infrastructure, clearer ownership, and safer migrations. Anti-patterns - Deploy production resources manually in the portal. This couples unrelated change rates and expands blast radius. - Do not hide remote calls, unbounded work, or mutable global state behind convenience helpers. - Do not introduce a distributed boundary without an owner, SLO, timeout, and failure policy. Enterprise considerations Assign owners to every boundary and data class. Enforce policy as code, retain architecture decisions and deployment evidence, and design regional, tenant, and regulatory isolation before data is written. Official guidance - Azure Architecture Center - Azure Well-Architected Framework - Managed identities Checklist - [ ] Domain and infrastructure boundaries are visible in code and telemetry. - [ ] Trust, data, transaction, and rollback boundaries are documented. - [ ] Dependency failure is bounded and tested. - [ ] Contract evolution is backward compatible. - [ ] Ownership and SLO are assigned. Changelog - 1.0.0 (2026-07-16): Added production architecture pattern.

docs.title: Docker Architecture Patterns
docs.description: Define the default production architecture for a Docker workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve.
docs.text: Docker Architecture Patterns Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define the default production architecture for a Docker workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve. Why Build minimal immutable images from pinned inputs, run as non-root, and keep secrets out of layers and build arguments. A stable boundary reduces coupling, limits failure propagation, and makes ownership auditable. How Use Multi-stage immutable image: Separate dependency, build, test, and minimal runtime stages; copy only runtime artifacts. Boundary rules 1. Validate identity, authorization, and input before domain mutation. 2. Keep dependency-specific types behind the infrastructure port. 3. Attach deadlines, cancellation, idempotency, and retry classification at the call boundary. 4. Emit traceable outcomes without secret or regulated payload leakage. 5. Version contracts and migrate producers before removing compatibility. Tradeoffs The extra adapter and contract code costs initial delivery time. It buys isolated tests, replaceable infrastructure, clearer ownership, and safer migrations. Anti-patterns - Install compilers and package caches in the runtime image. This couples unrelated change rates and expands blast radius. - Do not hide remote calls, unbounded work, or mutable global state behind convenience helpers. - Do not introduce a distributed boundary without an owner, SLO, timeout, and failure policy. Enterprise considerations Assign owners to every boundary and data class. Enforce policy as code, retain architecture decisions and deployment evidence, and design regional, tenant, and regulatory isolation before data is written. Official guidance - Dockerfile reference - Docker build best practices - Docker security Checklist - [ ] Domain and infrastructure boundaries are visible in code and telemetry. - [ ] Trust, data, transaction, and rollback boundaries are documented. - [ ] Dependency failure is bounded and tested. - [ ] Contract evolution is backward compatible. - [ ] Ownership and SLO are assigned. docs.title: Docker Common Error Workflow
docs.description: Diagnose recurring Docker failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error.
docs.text: Docker Common Error Workflow Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Diagnose recurring Docker failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error. Why Error text is a symptom, not a root cause. This workflow requires a discriminating observation before each repair. How 1. Preserve timestamps, correlation identifiers, artifact version, topology, and recent changes. 2. Stabilize user impact with the smallest reversible mitigation. 3. Capture the evidence named below before restarting or clearing state. 4. Test one ranked hypothesis at a time. 5. Add a regression test, alert, or policy after confirming root cause. Symptom Likely causal class Required repair Primary evidence --- --- --- --- exec format error Image architecture or entrypoint executable format mismatches the runtime. Build for the target platform and verify shebang and line endings. docker image inspect permission denied at startup The runtime user cannot read or write required paths. Create and chown only required paths during build. docker run with target user no space left on device Layers, build cache, logs, or writable data exhausted storage. Measure Docker disk use and apply retention without deleting active data. docker system df container exits with code 137 The process was SIGKILLed, commonly by an OOM limit. Inspect runtime OOM state and reduce memory or set evidence-based limits. docker inspect service cannot resolve Compose peer Services are not on the same network or use the wrong hostname. Use the Compose service name on a shared declared network. docker compose config 1. exec format error Confirm: Capture docker image inspect and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Image architecture or entrypoint executable format mismatches the runtime. Repair: Build for the target platform and verify shebang and line endings. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 2. permission denied at startup Confirm: Capture docker run with target user and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: The runtime user cannot read or write required paths. Repair: Create and chown only required paths during build. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 3. no space left on device Confirm: Capture docker system df and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Layers, build cache, logs, or writable data exhausted storage. Repair: Measure Docker disk use and apply retention without deleting active data. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 4. container exits with code 137 Confirm: Capture docker inspect and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: The process was SIGKILLed, commonly by an OOM limit. Repair: Inspect runtime OOM state and reduce memory or set evidence-based limits. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 5. service cannot resolve Compose peer Confirm: Capture docker compose config and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Services are not on the same network or use the wrong hostname. Repair: Use the Compose service name on a shared declared network. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. Tradeoffs This standard favors explicit contracts and deterministic validation over rapid, implicit configuration. It adds review work up front but reduces production ambiguity and rollback time. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated diagnostic or repair without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - Dockerfile reference - Docker build best practices - Docker security Checklist - [ ] Incident timeline and affected artifact identity are preserved. - [ ] Root cause explains every material observation. - [ ] Mitigation is reversible and does not destroy forensic state. - [ ] Permanent fix has a regression test. - [ ] Recovery is confirmed through user-impact telemetry. docs.text: .NET Common Error Workflow Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Diagnose recurring .NET failures from evidence and restore service without destructive trial and error. Why Error text is a symptom, not a root cause. This workflow requires a discriminating observation before each repair. How 1. Preserve timestamps, correlation identifiers, artifact version, topology, and recent changes. 2. Stabilize user impact with the smallest reversible mitigation. 3. Capture the evidence named below before restarting or clearing state. 4. Test one ranked hypothesis at a time. 5. Add a regression test, alert, or policy after confirming root cause. Symptom Likely causal class Required repair Primary evidence --- --- --- --- Cannot consume scoped service from singleton Dependency injection lifetimes are incompatible. Create an explicit scope per operation or correct the consumer lifetime. DI validation A second operation was started on this context Concurrent work shares one DbContext. Await each operation or create independent scopes. EF Core logs Possible object cycle detected API serialization traverses cyclic entity graphs. Map entities to bounded response DTOs. ASP.NET Core logs TaskCanceledException Request cancellation and upstream timeout are conflated. Inspect the caller token and classify timeout separately. distributed trace Configuration value is null Options were not bound or validated. Bind one options object and ValidateOnStart. startup logs 1. Cannot consume scoped service from singleton Confirm: Capture DI validation and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Dependency injection lifetimes are incompatible. Repair: Create an explicit scope per operation or correct the consumer lifetime. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 2. A second operation was started on this context Confirm: Capture EF Core logs and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Concurrent work shares one DbContext. Repair: Await each operation or create independent scopes. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 3. Possible object cycle detected Confirm: Capture ASP.NET Core logs and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: API serialization traverses cyclic entity graphs. Repair: Map entities to bounded response DTOs. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 4. TaskCanceledException Confirm: Capture distributed trace and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Request cancellation and upstream timeout are conflated. Repair: Inspect the caller token and classify timeout separately. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. 5. Configuration value is null Confirm: Capture startup logs and correlate it to the failing request, resource, or deployment revision. Cause: Options were not bound or validated. Verify: Reproduce the original operation, prove the error signal is absent, prove the intended result is present, and watch the relevant saturation/error metric for one complete operational window. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. Official guidance - .NET documentation - ASP.NET Core fundamentals - EF Core documentation Checklist - [ ] Incident timeline and affected artifact identity are preserved. - [ ] Root cause explains every material observation. - [ ] Mitigation is reversible and does not destroy forensic state. - [ ] Permanent fix has a regression test. - [ ] Recovery is confirmed through user-impact telemetry. docs.text: .NET Production Skill Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Provide a deterministic procedure for generating, changing, diagnosing, or releasing a ASP.NET Core endpoint, service, background worker, or EF Core operation with AI assistance. Trigger Activate when a request changes .NET source, configuration, infrastructure, data contracts, or production behavior. Do not activate for a documentation-only mention with no technical decision. Why Use request-scoped units of work, propagate CancellationToken, bind validated options, and keep transport models out of the domain. The skill converts that principle into evidence gates that an agent cannot skip. Inputs - Repository rules and ownership boundaries. - Exact runtime/toolchain evidence from manifests or platform APIs. - Requested behavior and acceptance tests. - Sanitized logs, traces, metrics, plans, or screenshots when diagnosing. - Deployment topology, SLO, data classification, and rollback mechanism. How 1. Discover the nearest repository instructions and established implementation pattern. 2. State the invariant, trust boundary, failure mode, and rollback boundary. 3. Select the matching prompt under ../prompts/. 4. Make the smallest coherent change; preserve public contracts unless migration is approved. 5. Run native formatting, static analysis, unit/integration tests, security checks, and build/package validation. 6. Apply ../checklists/code-review.md. 7. For release work, apply ../checklists/deployment.md and capture evidence. Verification 1. Verify that CancellationToken reaches I/O. 2. Verify that DI lifetimes are valid. 3. Verify that queries avoid accidental client evaluation and N+1. 4. Verify that configuration is validated at startup. 5. Record commands, exit status, artifact identity, and links to retained evidence. Communication protocol Report decisions, changed files, commands actually run, observed results, residual risks, and an explicit ship/block recommendation. Distinguish facts from hypotheses. Termination criteria Finish only when acceptance tests and both relevant checklists pass, or when a named blocker with owner and required evidence is recorded. Anti-patterns - Do not accept generated ASP.NET Core endpoint, service, background worker, or EF Core operation without executing the technology's native validators. - Do not suppress diagnostics without recording the violated invariant and compensating control. - Do not introduce a dependency when the platform already provides the required capability. Enterprise considerations Record artifact provenance, reviewer identity, test evidence, security findings, and deployment approval. Redact credentials and regulated data before sending context to an AI system. Enforce the same policy, audit, retention, and separation-of-duties controls used for human-authored changes. docs.text: GraphQL Architecture Patterns Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define the default production architecture for a GraphQL workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve. Why Design schema around domain capabilities, authorize at trusted boundaries, batch data access per request, and enforce operation budgets. A stable boundary reduces coupling, limits failure propagation, and makes ownership auditable. How Use Schema-owned domain boundary: Each domain owns types and resolvers; a gateway composes contracts while services retain authorization. Boundary rules 1. Validate identity, authorization, and input before domain mutation. 2. Keep dependency-specific types behind the infrastructure port. 3. Attach deadlines, cancellation, idempotency, and retry classification at the call boundary. 4. Emit traceable outcomes without secret or regulated payload leakage. 5. Version contracts and migrate producers before removing compatibility. Tradeoffs The extra adapter and contract code costs initial delivery time. It buys isolated tests, replaceable infrastructure, clearer ownership, and safer migrations. Anti-patterns - Expose database tables one-to-one as schema types. This couples unrelated change rates and expands blast radius. - Do not hide remote calls, unbounded work, or mutable global state behind convenience helpers. - Do not introduce a distributed boundary without an owner, SLO, timeout, and failure policy. Enterprise considerations Assign owners to every boundary and data class. Enforce policy as code, retain architecture decisions and deployment evidence, and design regional, tenant, and regulatory isolation before data is written. Official guidance - GraphQL specification - GraphQL learn - OWASP GraphQL cheat sheet Checklist - [ ] Domain and infrastructure boundaries are visible in code and telemetry. - [ ] Trust, data, transaction, and rollback boundaries are documented. - [ ] Dependency failure is bounded and tested. - [ ] Contract evolution is backward compatible. - [ ] Ownership and SLO are assigned. Trigger Activate when a request changes GraphQL source, configuration, infrastructure, data contracts, or production behavior. Select the matching prompt under ../prompts/. 4. Make the smallest coherent change; preserve public contracts unless migration is approved. 5. Run native formatting, static analysis, unit/integration tests, security checks, and build/package validation. 6. Apply ../checklists/code-review.md. 7. docs.description: Define the default production architecture for a Java workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve.
docs.text: Java Architecture Patterns Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Define the default production architecture for a Java workload and the boundaries an AI-generated change must preserve. Why Put transactions around use cases, keep entities out of transport contracts, and make blocking resource limits explicit. A stable boundary reduces coupling, limits failure propagation, and makes ownership auditable. How Use Transactional application service: Controllers map DTOs; application services own transactions; repositories persist aggregates. Boundary rules 1. Validate identity, authorization, and input before domain mutation. 2. Keep dependency-specific types behind the infrastructure port. 3. Attach deadlines, cancellation, idempotency, and retry classification at the call boundary. 4. Emit traceable outcomes without secret or regulated payload leakage. 5. Version contracts and migrate producers before removing compatibility. Tradeoffs The extra adapter and contract code costs initial delivery time. It buys isolated tests, replaceable infrastructure, clearer ownership, and safer migrations. Anti-patterns - Expose JPA entities as API payloads. This couples unrelated change rates and expands blast radius. - Do not hide remote calls, unbounded work, or mutable global state behind convenience helpers. - Do not introduce a distributed boundary without an owner, SLO, timeout, and failure policy. Enterprise considerations Assign owners to every boundary and data class. Enforce policy as code, retain architecture decisions and deployment evidence, and design regional, tenant, and regulatory isolation before data is written. Official guidance - Java documentation - Spring Boot reference - Spring transaction management Checklist - [ ] Domain and infrastructure boundaries are visible in code and telemetry. - [ ] Trust, data, transaction, and rollback boundaries are documented. - [ ] Dependency failure is bounded and tested. - [ ] Contract evolution is backward compatible. - [ ] Ownership and SLO are assigned.
