docs.text: React Native Production Skill Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose Provide a deterministic procedure for generating, changing, diagnosing, or releasing a screen, native module boundary, navigation flow, list, or mobile release with AI assistance. Do not activate for a documentation-only mention with no technical decision. Why Share domain logic, not platform assumptions; keep native boundaries typed, virtualize long lists, and test on representative devices. The skill converts that principle into evidence gates that an agent cannot skip. Inputs - Repository rules and ownership boundaries. - Exact runtime/toolchain evidence from manifests or platform APIs. - Requested behavior and acceptance tests. - Sanitized logs, traces, metrics, plans, or screenshots when diagnosing. - Deployment topology, SLO, data classification, and rollback mechanism. How 1. Discover the nearest repository instructions and established implementation pattern. 2. State the invariant, trust boundary, failure mode, and rollback boundary. 3. Select the matching prompt under ../prompts/. 4. Make the smallest coherent change; preserve public contracts unless migration is approved. 5. Run native formatting, static analysis, unit/integration tests, security checks, and build/package validation. 6. Apply ../checklists/code-review.md. 7. For release work, apply ../checklists/deployment.md and capture evidence. Verification 1. Verify that platform behavior is explicit. 2. Verify that native boundary is typed and failure-safe. 3. Verify that lists are virtualized and measured. 4. Verify that screen-reader labels and focus order are tested. 5. Record commands, exit status, artifact identity, and links to retained evidence. Unhappy path and recovery - If repository or version evidence is missing, stop and request it. - If a validator fails, fix the first causal error; never suppress the rule as the initial response. - If the failure cannot be reproduced, improve telemetry and preserve the incident state. - If a release gate fails, halt progression and execute the documented rollback or feature-disable path. - If credentials or regulated data appear in context, stop, revoke or rotate as required, and follow incident policy. Communication protocol Report decisions, changed files, commands actually run, observed results, residual risks, and an explicit ship/block recommendation. Distinguish facts from hypotheses. Termination criteria Finish only when acceptance tests and both relevant checklists pass, or when a named blocker with owner and required evidence is recorded. docs.text: AI Cookbook Version: 1.0.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Purpose The AI Cookbook provides 18 production playbooks that constrain AI-assisted engineering with technology-specific invariants, diagnostics, architecture, and release gates. Why Generic prompts miss runtime-specific failure modes. These cookbooks tie generation and review to official guidance, repository evidence, deterministic validation, and production ownership. How 1. Select the cookbook matching the system boundary being changed. 2. Supply repository and runtime evidence to one of its three XML prompts. 3. Execute the procedural skill and native validators. 4. Diagnose observed failures through the evidence-led error workflow. 5. Block merge and deployment until the corresponding checklists pass. Complete cookbooks Technology Production scope --- --- React Components, Hooks, state, accessibility, rendering Next.js App Router, server/client boundaries, caching, streaming Node.js APIs, async control flow, process lifecycle, observability Python Typed services, async boundaries, packaging, diagnostics Java Spring, transactions, persistence, JVM operations .NET ASP.NET Core, DI, EF Core, cancellation Azure Identity, networking, IaC, policy, reliability AWS IAM, accounts, IaC, reliability, quotas Docker Reproducible images, least privilege, supply chain Kubernetes Controllers, probes, resources, policy, rollouts PostgreSQL Schemas, plans, transactions, migrations, recovery Redis Cache semantics, data structures, memory, clustering MongoDB Document models, indexes, aggregation, sharding GraphQL Schema contracts, resolvers, authorization, budgets Microfrontends Domain ownership, composition, contracts, isolation React Native Native boundaries, navigation, lists, accessibility Performance Engineering SLOs, profiling, budgets, capacity, regression gates Accessibility Engineering WCAG, semantics, keyboard, focus, assistive technology Count reconciliation The previous table contained 19 rows while the repository claimed 18 technology stacks. Do not activate for a documentation-only mention with no technical decision. Why Treat Redis as a bounded data-structure server: define ownership, TTL, memory policy, consistency, and failure behavior for every keyspace. The skill converts that principle into evidence gates that an agent cannot skip. Inputs - Repository rules and ownership boundaries. - Exact runtime/toolchain evidence from manifests or platform APIs. - Requested behavior and acceptance tests. - Sanitized logs, traces, metrics, plans, or screenshots when diagnosing. - Deployment topology, SLO, data classification, and rollback mechanism. How 1. Discover the nearest repository instructions and established implementation pattern. 2. State the invariant, trust boundary, failure mode, and rollback boundary. 3. Select the matching prompt under ../prompts/. 4. Make the smallest coherent change; preserve public contracts unless migration is approved. 5. Run native formatting, static analysis, unit/integration tests, security checks, and build/package validation. 6. Apply ../checklists/code-review.md. 7. docs.title: Chrome DevTools MCP Integration
docs.description: Provide agent-safe access to isolated pages, DOM, console, network, performance traces. Use this integration only when those capabilities are required and a nam
docs.text: Chrome DevTools MCP Integration Version: 1.1 Updated: 2026-07-16 Category: Browser/Testing Purpose and applicability Provide agent-safe access to isolated pages, DOM, console, network, performance traces. Use this integration only when those capabilities are required and a named owner accepts the data and write risk. The implementation baseline is Google Chrome's official chrome-devtools-mcp package. Protocol, transport, and capability lifecycle Implement stable MCP 2025-11-25. Negotiate protocolVersion in initialize; reject unsupported versions. Prefer Streamable HTTP for remote service and stdio only for a local, single-user process; do not expose stdio through a network shim. Advertise only implemented tools, resources, prompts, and logging. Paginate lists, use progress/cancellation where supported, and send the corresponding listchanged notification after authorization or configuration changes. Clients re-list and review metadata changes before use. Tool, resource, and prompt design - Tools: bounded list/get/search operations over isolated pages, DOM, console, network, performance traces; mutations are separate, disabled by default, idempotency-aware, and approval-gated. - Resources: canonical read-only URIs scoped to tenant/session/Chrome profile; stable IDs and versions replace display names where possible. - Prompts: vendor-specific triage/review prompts return instructions and resource links only; prompts never silently invoke tools. - Validation: closed JSON Schemas; normalize and authorize allowed origins, URLs, request bodies, trace size, and timeout; cap arrays, strings, time ranges, rows, bytes, and pagination. Return typed, size-bounded results with opaque cursors and structured errors. Label all provider content untrusted and redact credentials, secrets, personal data, and internal URLs. Authorization, consent, and least privilege Remote deployments publish RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata and standards-compliant WWW-Authenticate. Discover the authorization server from metadata, require authorization code flow with PKCE S256, verify advertised PKCE support, and include the canonical MCP URI as RFC 8707 resource in authorization and token requests. Validate token signature, issuer, expiry/not-before, authorized party when applicable, and audience/resource for this server. Never pass an inbound MCP bearer token to the provider. Exchange/map it server-side to a short-lived, tenant-bound provider credential. Consent names the provider, tenant, enabled tools, data classes, and write effects. Use local process policy; remote servers use MCP OAuth and isolated Chrome profiles; rely on the provider's current permission catalog and consent screen—never invent scope names. Step-up authorization cannot silently broaden prior consent. Threat controls Risk Mandatory control --- --- Prompt injection Treat provider/web/database text as data; instructions in results cannot authorize calls or alter policy. Tool poisoning Pin package/image and provenance; allowlist tools; diff descriptions/schemas on change before activation. Exfiltration Enforce tenant/object allowlists, DLP/redaction, egress policy, response caps, and approval for cross-boundary transfer. SSRF Fixed provider origins, DNS/IP checks, redirect revalidation, private/link-local denial, and no arbitrary URL fetch tool. Unsafe writes Policy plus provider authorization, exact-argument approval, concurrency checks, idempotency key where supported, and no blind retry. Operations, tenancy, and incidents Rate-limit against session/action/trace budgets and target-site response signals. Do not claim a fixed limit where the provider makes limits endpoint-, plan-, or tenant-dependent. Apply budgets per user/tenant/tool, bounded jittered backoff for idempotent reads, circuit breaking, and surfaced retry times. Emit OpenTelemetry metrics/spans for tool, tenant hash, status, latency, bytes, pagination, approval ID, provider request ID, and rate-limit state; never record tokens or raw content. Partition credentials, caches, cursors, browser/database sessions, telemetry, and audit records by tenant/session/Chrome profile. Re-authorize on tenant change. Revocation disables the grant immediately, removes provider credentials, terminates sessions, and evicts credential-bound caches. Incident response: disable risky tools, revoke/rotate credentials, preserve tamper-evident audit evidence, identify tenants/calls/data, contain egress, notify owners under policy, patch and adversarially retest before staged restoration. Verification - Contract-test initialization/version failure, capability declarations/change, schemas, pagination, cancellation, errors, and output caps. - Test RFC 9728 discovery, PKCE downgrade refusal, RFC 8707 resource binding, issuer/audience/expiry rejection, no token passthrough, consent, revocation, and tenant isolation. - Attack-test injected content, poisoned tool metadata, DNS rebinding/redirect SSRF, oversized/secret output, confused deputy, approval replay, cross-tenant cursors, and rate-limit exhaustion. - Test read and write paths in a disposable tenant; prove provider authorization and rollback/compensation behavior. Tradeoffs Deep debugging visibility improves diagnosis but exposes cookies, headers, and page secrets. Least-privilege tool selection reduces agent flexibility and requires ongoing permission and schema maintenance. Anti-patterns - Broad administrator credentials, undocumented scopes/quotas, shared cross-tenant sessions, or secrets in config/logs. - Exposing the provider API one-for-one, enabling all tools, trusting returned instructions, or treating model confirmation as durable approval. - Retrying writes after ambiguous failure, accepting arbitrary URLs/queries/paths, or logging complete payloads. Enterprise considerations Enforce managed Chrome versions, isolated disposable profiles, remote-debugging endpoint isolation, egress allowlists, test-account governance, network/trace redaction, artifact retention, and prohibition on attaching to employee browsing sessions. Enforce separation of duties, legal hold and accessibility requirements where applicable; pin releases, verify provenance/SBOMs, stage upgrades, and document RTO/RPO plus outage behavior. Checklist - [ ] Implementation and transports approved; MCP negotiation and capability change tested - [ ] Tools/resources/prompts bounded; input/output validation and write approvals enforced - [ ] RFC 9728, PKCE S256, RFC 8707, issuer/audience validation, consent, and least privilege verified - [ ] No token passthrough; injection, exfiltration, SSRF, and tool-poisoning defenses tested - [ ] Provider-aware limits, redacted telemetry, tenancy, revocation, and incident runbook operational - [ ] Tradeoffs, enterprise controls, contract/integration/adversarial tests accepted Primary references - Chrome DevTools implementation/API - Chrome DevTools limits/security - MCP specification 2025-11-25 - MCP authorization Changelog - 1.1 — 2026-07-16: Replaced a template marker with concrete service-specific enterprise controls. - 1.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production specification.

docs.text: MCP Integration Standard Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Protocol baseline: MCP 2025-11-25 Purpose Define the production contract for connecting agents to external systems through Model Context Protocol (MCP). This inventory provides exactly 24 service-specific specifications with implementation, authorization, threat, operations, enterprise, and verification requirements. Why MCP removes client-by-service integration duplication, but protocol compatibility does not make an integration safe. Tool metadata can be poisoned, provider content can inject instructions, broad credentials can create confused deputies, and remote servers introduce OAuth, tenancy, egress, and incident-response obligations. These specifications make those controls explicit and testable. How to use this standard 1. Select the service specification from the inventory and confirm its applicability and official implementation status. 2. Enable only tools, resources, and prompts required by the approved use case. The correct number is determined by task need, client context budget, authorization surface, and evaluation evidence—not a universal numeric maximum. 3. Separate reads from mutations. Require policy evaluation and human approval bound to the exact arguments for consequential writes. 4. Implement the authorization profile below for remote servers; keep local stdio servers local and single-user. 5. Validate schemas, provider identifiers, destinations, outputs, pagination, and size/cost limits. Treat all retrieved content as untrusted data. 6. Verify contract, integration, authorization, tenant-isolation, adversarial, revocation, and incident tests before production. Protocol and capability lifecycle - Negotiate protocolVersion during initialize; support MCP 2025-11-25 or fail explicitly. - Use Streamable HTTP for remote servers. Use stdio only for a local child process; never expose it through an unauthenticated network wrapper. - Advertise only implemented capabilities. Paginate lists and implement cancellation/progress where the operation warrants it. - Send the applicable notifications/tools/listchanged, notifications/resources/listchanged, or notifications/prompts/listchanged notification after a material catalog or entitlement change. Clients must re-list and review changed metadata before use. - Prefer official vendor-hosted servers or vendor-maintained packages. Pin local packages/images and verify release provenance; a community server requires an explicit security review and named maintainer. Authorization profile for remote MCP servers MCP 2025-11-25 remote authorization is an OAuth protected-resource flow, not provider-token forwarding: 1. The MCP server publishes OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata under RFC 9728 and returns a standards-compliant WWW-Authenticate challenge. 2. The client discovers an authorization server only through validated protected-resource and authorization-server metadata. 3. Authorization code flow uses PKCE. The client verifies advertised support and uses S256; it refuses authorization when required PKCE metadata is absent. 4. The client includes the canonical MCP server URI as the RFC 8707 resource value in both authorization and token requests. 5. The MCP server validates token signature, issuer, expiry/not-before, authorized party when applicable, and audience/resource. A token for another resource is rejected. 6. The MCP server never passes the inbound MCP bearer token through to the downstream provider. It uses a server-side exchange or maps the identity to a separate short-lived, tenant-bound provider credential. 7. Consent identifies the service, tenant, enabled capabilities, data classes, and write effects. Step-up authorization cannot silently broaden previous consent. Local servers that use environment credentials still require least privilege, secret-manager delivery, rotation, process isolation, and provider-side authorization. They must not claim compliance with the remote OAuth profile unless they implement it. Tool, resource, and prompt design - Tool names describe intent; descriptions state when to use the tool, side effects, approval needs, and important limits. - Inputs use closed JSON Schemas, bounded strings/arrays/time ranges, canonical provider IDs, explicit pagination, and destination allowlists. - Outputs are typed, bounded, redacted, and labeled as untrusted. Return stable IDs, source references, provider request IDs, and structured errors. - Resources are read-only, canonical, tenant-scoped, and versioned where the provider permits. Prompts return instructions and resource references; they do not silently execute writes. - Provider text, code, logs, tickets, messages, pages, traces, database values, and web content cannot authorize another tool call or override system policy. Security and privacy controls Risk Required control --- --- Prompt injection Preserve trust boundaries, label external content, isolate instructions from data, and evaluate adversarial content. Tool poisoning Pin provenance, allowlist tools, diff names/descriptions/schemas after change notifications, and require review before activation. Data exfiltration Object and tenant allowlists, DLP/redaction, egress policy, response caps, and approval for cross-boundary movement. SSRF Fixed provider origins, DNS/IP and redirect revalidation, private/link-local denial, and no arbitrary URL-fetch primitive. Confused deputy User/tenant-bound credentials, provider authorization on every operation, exact-argument approvals, and audience validation. Unsafe mutation Optimistic concurrency, idempotency where supported, no blind write retry, and rollback or compensation testing. Rate limits, telemetry, and audit Use each provider's documented response headers, cost model, retry signals, and endpoint/plan limits; do not invent a fixed quota. Apply per-user, per-tenant, and per-tool budgets, bounded exponential backoff with jitter for idempotent reads, circuit breaking, and explicit handling of ambiguous writes. Record enough metadata to reconstruct authorization and operational decisions: timestamp, actor/tenant pseudonym, tool, outcome, latency, bytes, provider request ID, approval reference, policy decision, and rate-limit state. Do not universally log raw inputs or outputs. Capture content only when an approved purpose, classification, minimization rule, access control, retention period, and redaction policy require it. Never log bearer tokens, provider credentials, secrets, or unrestricted payloads. Tenancy, revocation, and incident response Partition credentials, caches, cursors, sessions, telemetry, and audit records by the service's tenant boundary. Re-authorize tenant changes. Revocation must disable the MCP grant immediately, remove provider credentials, terminate active sessions, and evict credential-bound caches. Incident runbooks must support disabling risky tools, revoking/rotating credentials, preserving tamper-evident evidence, identifying affected tenants/calls/data, containing egress, notifying owners under policy, patching, adversarial retesting, and staged restoration. Inventory Version Control - GitHub - GitLab - Azure DevOps - Bitbucket Cloud Project Management - Jira Cloud - Linear - Notion - Asana - monday.com Communication - Slack - Microsoft Teams - Discord Infrastructure and Data - Filesystem - Docker - Kubernetes - PostgreSQL - Redis - Supabase Observability - Sentry - Datadog - Grafana - OpenTelemetry Browser and Testing - Playwright - Chrome DevTools Tradeoffs MCP standardizes discovery and invocation but adds another authorization and supply-chain boundary. Official hosted servers reduce adapter drift while introducing vendor availability and data-path dependencies. Narrow catalogs and approvals reduce agent autonomy and add latency, but they constrain blast radius and make behavior auditable. Anti-patterns - Forwarding the MCP access token to a provider, accepting a token minted for another audience, or inventing provider scope names. - Treating every provider endpoint as a tool, enforcing an arbitrary global tool-count limit, or loading catalogs without evaluation. - Trusting instructions returned by tools/resources, accepting arbitrary destinations, or sharing credentials/cursors across tenants. - Logging all raw inputs and outputs by default, retrying writes after ambiguous failures, or enabling destructive tools through model confirmation alone. Enterprise considerations Integrate SSO/SCIM, separation of duties, approved-app workflows, DLP, audit export, retention/deletion, legal hold, eDiscovery, accessibility, residency, and incident notification according to each service specification and data classification. Maintain an owner, data-flow record, threat model, vendor review, SBOM/provenance record, upgrade policy, RTO/RPO, credential inventory, and tested decommission path for every deployment. Checklist - [ ] One inventory specification and named owner selected - [ ] MCP version, transport, capabilities, pagination, cancellation, and change notifications tested - [ ] RFC 9728 discovery, PKCE S256, RFC 8707 binding, issuer/audience validation, and no token passthrough verified - [ ] Consent, least privilege, provider authorization, and argument-bound mutation approval tested - [ ] Input/output validation, injection, exfiltration, SSRF, tool poisoning, and confused-deputy tests pass - [ ] Provider-aware rate controls and minimized, redacted telemetry are operational - [ ] Tenant isolation, revocation, incident response, enterprise controls, and decommissioning are tested - [ ] Package/image provenance, citations, inventory count, and links are current Primary references - MCP specification 2025-11-25 - MCP authorization - OAuth 2.0 Protected Resource Metadata — RFC 9728 - Resource Indicators for OAuth 2.0 — RFC 8707 - Proof Key for Code Exchange — RFC 7636 - OAuth 2.0 Security Best Current Practice — RFC 9700 Changelog - 2.0 — 2026-07-16: Replaced legacy universal tool-count and payload-logging claims; added the MCP 2025-11-25 authorization profile, capability lifecycle, threat controls, enterprise requirements, citations, and verified 24-file inventory. - 1.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial integration inventory.

Return typed, size-bounded results with opaque cursors and structured errors. Label all provider content untrusted and redact credentials, secrets, personal data, and internal URLs. Authorization, consent, and least privilege Remote deployments publish RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata and standards-compliant WWW-Authenticate. Discover the authorization server from metadata, require authorization code flow with PKCE S256, verify advertised PKCE support, and include the canonical MCP URI as RFC 8707 resource in authorization and token requests. Validate token signature, issuer, expiry/not-before, authorized party when applicable, and audience/resource for this server. Never pass an inbound MCP bearer token to the provider. Exchange/map it server-side to a short-lived, tenant-bound provider credential. Consent names the provider, tenant, enabled tools, data classes, and write effects. Use Atlassian consent and Bitbucket workspace/repository permissions; rely on the provider's current permission catalog and consent screen—never invent scope names. Step-up authorization cannot silently broaden prior consent. Threat controls Risk Mandatory control --- --- Prompt injection Treat provider/web/database text as data; instructions in results cannot authorize calls or alter policy. Tool poisoning Pin package/image and provenance; allowlist tools; diff descriptions/schemas on change before activation. Exfiltration Enforce tenant/object allowlists, DLP/redaction, egress policy, response caps, and approval for cross-boundary transfer. SSRF Fixed provider origins, DNS/IP checks, redirect revalidation, private/link-local denial, and no arbitrary URL fetch tool. Unsafe writes Policy plus provider authorization, exact-argument approval, concurrency checks, idempotency key where supported, and no blind retry. Operations, tenancy, and incidents Rate-limit against Bitbucket X-RateLimit- headers and official endpoint documentation. Do not claim a fixed limit where the provider makes limits endpoint-, plan-, or tenant-dependent. Apply budgets per user/tenant/tool, bounded jittered backoff for idempotent reads, circuit breaking, and surfaced retry times. Emit OpenTelemetry metrics/spans for tool, tenant hash, status, latency, bytes, pagination, approval ID, provider request ID, and rate-limit state; never record tokens or raw content. Partition credentials, caches, cursors, browser/database sessions, telemetry, and audit records by Atlassian site/workspace/repository. Re-authorize on tenant change. Revocation disables the grant immediately, removes provider credentials, terminates sessions, and evicts credential-bound caches. Incident response: disable risky tools, revoke/rotate credentials, preserve tamper-evident audit evidence, identify tenants/calls/data, contain egress, notify owners under policy, patch and adversarially retest before staged restoration. Verification - Contract-test initialization/version failure, capability declarations/change, schemas, pagination, cancellation, errors, and output caps. - Test RFC 9728 discovery, PKCE downgrade refusal, RFC 8707 resource binding, issuer/audience/expiry rejection, no token passthrough, consent, revocation, and tenant isolation. - Attack-test injected content, poisoned tool metadata, DNS rebinding/redirect SSRF, oversized/secret output, confused deputy, approval replay, cross-tenant cursors, and rate-limit exhaustion. - Test read and write paths in a disposable tenant; prove provider authorization and rollback/compensation behavior. Tradeoffs The Atlassian service centralizes identity but expands the trust boundary across products. Least-privilege tool selection reduces agent flexibility and requires ongoing permission and schema maintenance. Anti-patterns - Broad administrator credentials, undocumented scopes/quotas, shared cross-tenant sessions, or secrets in config/logs. - Exposing the provider API one-for-one, enabling all tools, trusting returned instructions, or treating model confirmation as durable approval. - Retrying writes after ambiguous failure, accepting arbitrary URLs/queries/paths, or logging complete payloads. Enterprise considerations Enforce Atlassian Guard SAML/SCIM, managed accounts, workspace access controls, branch restrictions, audit-log export, data residency, and organization-approved app access. Enforce separation of duties, legal hold and accessibility requirements where applicable; pin releases, verify provenance/SBOMs, stage upgrades, and document RTO/RPO plus outage behavior. Checklist - [ ] Implementation and transports approved; MCP negotiation and capability change tested - [ ] Tools/resources/prompts bounded; input/output validation and write approvals enforced - [ ] RFC 9728, PKCE S256, RFC 8707, issuer/audience validation, consent, and least privilege verified - [ ] No token passthrough; injection, exfiltration, SSRF, and tool-poisoning defenses tested - [ ] Provider-aware limits, redacted telemetry, tenancy, revocation, and incident runbook operational - [ ] Tradeoffs, enterprise controls, contract/integration/adversarial tests accepted Primary references - Bitbucket Cloud implementation/API - Bitbucket Cloud limits/security - MCP specification 2025-11-25 - MCP authorization Changelog - 1.1 — 2026-07-16: Replaced a template marker with concrete service-specific enterprise controls. - 1.0 — 2026-07-16: Initial production specification.

docs.title: GitHub MCP Integration
docs.description: Connect agents to GitHub repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions, and security findings through GitHub's official MCP server. Use it for bounded software-d
docs.text: GitHub MCP Integration Version: 2.1 Updated: 2026-07-16 Owner: Platform Engineering Purpose Connect agents to GitHub repositories, issues, pull requests, Actions, and security findings through GitHub's official MCP server. Use it for bounded software-delivery workflows; do not use it as an unrestricted GitHub API proxy. Applicability Use the hosted server for GitHub.com and the official local server for GitHub Enterprise Server, private-network access, or controlled toolsets. Separate read-only analysis from write workflows and require approval before merge, workflow dispatch, settings, or content mutation. Protocol, implementation, transports, and capability lifecycle - Baseline MCP 2025-11-25; negotiate protocolVersion during initialize and reject unsupported revisions. - Prefer GitHub's hosted Streamable HTTP service. The official github/github-mcp-server supports local stdio and containers. - Enable only required toolsets; advertise tools, resources, prompts, and logging only when implemented. Emit notifications/tools/listchanged after an entitlement or configuration change. Tool, resource, and prompt design Primitive Contract --- --- Tools searchrepositories, getfilecontents, listissues, getpullrequest, createissue, addissuecomment; mutation tools are separately enabled and approval-gated. Resources Canonical, read-only URIs such as github://acme/payments/issues/123 and github://acme/payments/contents/src/main.ts?ref=4f3c2b1; immutable SHA references are preferred. Prompts triageissue and reviewpullrequest return instructions and bounded resource references, never execute writes. Inputs use closed JSON Schemas, normalized owner/repo, bounded result counts, SHA/ref validation, and repository allowlists. Outputs are size-bounded typed summaries with opaque pagination cursors; untrusted Markdown, diffs, comments, and logs are labeled as data and secrets are redacted. Authorization and consent Hosted deployments MUST publish RFC 9728 Protected Resource Metadata at the well-known URI and return a standards-compliant WWW-Authenticate challenge. Discover the authorization server from that metadata; use authorization code flow with PKCE S256, verify advertised PKCE support, and send the canonical MCP URI as RFC 8707 resource in both authorization and token requests. Validate signature, issuer, expiry, not-before, authorized party where applicable, and audience/resource against this MCP server. Never accept a GitHub token minted for another audience and never pass the inbound MCP bearer token through to GitHub. Exchange or map it server-side to a short-lived GitHub App installation token. Show repository/tool permissions and write impact at consent; request only permissions shown by GitHub for the selected toolsets. Do not invent or hard-code OAuth scope names. Keep per-user, per-installation credentials isolated and encrypted. Security controls Risk Required control --- --- Prompt injection/tool poisoning Treat repository text as untrusted; pin the official image/package; sign deployment manifests; diff tool metadata before accepting listchanged. Data exfiltration Repository/organization allowlists, output DLP, response-size limits, and approval for cross-repository transfer. SSRF Call only configured GitHub API/upload hosts; reject user-supplied absolute URLs, redirects to other origins, and private-address resolution. Destructive writes Branch protection remains authoritative; bind approval to exact tool arguments and expire it after one call. Operations Honor GitHub's primary and secondary rate-limit headers and GraphQL cost data; do not publish a fixed quota. Use bounded exponential backoff with jitter for idempotent reads, never blindly retry writes, and expose remaining-budget telemetry without tokens. Record OpenTelemetry spans with tool, hashed installation/repository, status, latency, pagination, rate-limit state, and approval ID; redact source, issue bodies, authorization headers, and tokens. Tenant keys are organization plus GitHub App installation; prevent cache, cursor, token, and audit-log crossover. Revoke by suspending/uninstalling the GitHub App, deleting server-side grants, invalidating sessions, and clearing credential-bound caches. Incident response: disable write toolsets, revoke installations/tokens, preserve tamper-evident audit records, identify affected repositories and calls, rotate secrets, notify owners, and re-enable after tested containment. Verification - Contract-test initialize/version negotiation, pagination, schemas, errors, and listchanged. - Verify RFC 9728 discovery, PKCE downgrade refusal, RFC 8707 binding, issuer/audience rejection, expiry, revocation, and tenant isolation. - Adversarially test malicious issue text, poisoned tool descriptions, redirect/DNS SSRF, secret-bearing diffs, oversized output, replayed approvals, and rate-limit recovery. - Run write tests only in an isolated GitHub organization with branch protection and assert no token passthrough. Tradeoffs The official server tracks GitHub features and reduces adapter drift, but its broad catalog increases context and authorization surface. Toolset allowlisting sacrifices coverage for predictable behavior. GitHub App installation tokens require administration but provide stronger repository isolation than personal access tokens. Anti-patterns - Using classic broad personal access tokens or copying MCP bearer tokens into GitHub API calls. - Loading every toolset, allowing model-selected repositories, or auto-merging after a text-only confirmation. - Logging diffs, comments, headers, or raw GraphQL responses as telemetry. Enterprise considerations Enforce GitHub Enterprise policies, SSO, IP allowlists, branch/rulesets, data residency, retention, legal hold, and audit export independently of the MCP server. Pin releases and images, generate an SBOM, verify provenance, stage upgrades, and assign organization-level owners for grants and incident response. Checklist - [ ] Official server pinned; tools and repositories allowlisted - [ ] MCP negotiation, change notifications, and schemas tested - [ ] RFC 9728, PKCE S256, RFC 8707, issuer/audience validation enforced - [ ] No token passthrough; short-lived GitHub App credentials used - [ ] Consent, least privilege, approval, DLP, SSRF, and injection controls verified - [ ] Rate-limit telemetry, tenant isolation, revocation, incidents, and adversarial tests operational Primary references - GitHub MCP Server - GitHub Apps authentication - GitHub REST rate limits - MCP authorization Changelog - 2.1 — 2026-07-16: Replaced template-style URI markers with concrete canonical examples. - 2.0 — 2026-07-16: Replaced the legacy PAT-oriented draft with a production hosted/local, OAuth, threat, operations, and verification specification.

docs.text: Context: Worked Production Example Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Scenario and artifacts Prepare context for changing tax rounding. docs.text: Debug: Workflow Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose Execute the domain method for isolate a software defect through reproducible observations and falsifiable experiments. Procedure 1. Write a deterministic. Write a deterministic symptom statement without assigning cause. 2. Capture a minimal. Capture a minimal reproduction and a known-good control. 3. Build a timeline. Build a timeline across logs, traces, deploys, and configuration. 4. Enumerate mutually distinguishable. Enumerate mutually distinguishable hypotheses. 5. Rank hypotheses by. Rank hypotheses by explanatory power and test cost. 6. Change one variable. Change one variable per experiment and preserve raw output. 7. Localize the causal. Localize the causal mechanism and add a failing regression test. 8. Apply the smallest. Apply the smallest fix; run focused, suite, and production guardrails. docs.text: Planner: Problem Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose The Planner pattern exists because teams need to turn ambiguous engineering work into a decision-complete execution contract, yet commonly act before the domain evidence can support that outcome. Observable problem 1. When more than three components change, an undocumented assumption can become a production decision. 2. When a dependency order constrains delivery, an undocumented assumption can become a production decision. 3. When an API, schema, or trust boundary changes, an undocumented assumption can become a production decision. Quality boundary The pattern is complete only when decision completeness = 100%; unplanned file-change rate < 10%; plan-driven rework < 10%; all critical-path owners acknowledge. Its scope excludes routine work that cannot trigger the stated failure modes. Tradeoffs A stricter entry test may defer work with weak evidence; proceeding would transfer unknown risk to operators and users. For the Planner problem contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "decision completeness = 100%"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Stop implementation, revert partial increments, and return to the last approved plan revision. Anti-patterns Do not rewrite a requested solution as the problem statement. State the violated invariant, affected population, baseline, target, and non-goals. For the Planner problem contract, gate 2 is evidenced by "decision completeness = 100%"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Stop implementation, revert partial increments, and return to the last approved plan revision. Enterprise considerations The accountable service owner accepts the problem statement; risk or compliance owners accept any material residual exposure. For the Planner problem contract, gate 3 is evidenced by "decision completeness = 100%"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Stop implementation, revert partial increments, and return to the last approved plan revision. docs.title: OAIES Pattern Library
docs.description: Provide twelve distinct production methods for consequential AI-assisted engineering. The thirteen files in each pattern are operational specifications, not ren
docs.text: OAIES Pattern Library Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose Provide twelve distinct production methods for consequential AI-assisted engineering. The thirteen files in each pattern are operational specifications, not renamed copies of a universal agent loop. Catalog Pattern Domain outcome Maturity --- --- --- Planner Turn ambiguous engineering work into a decision-complete execution contract Stable 2.0 Reviewer Detect consequential defects with requirement-traceable, severity-calibrated findings Stable 2.0 Context Construct a minimal, provenance-bearing information package that preserves decision quality Stable 2.0 Debug Isolate a software defect through reproducible observations and falsifiable experiments Stable 2.0 Migration Transition data or services while preserving invariants and a tested return path Stable 2.0 Legacy Modernization Replace obsolete internals incrementally while preserving observed business behavior Stable 2.0 Architecture Choose and govern a system design against quantified quality-attribute scenarios Stable 2.0 Optimization Improve a profiled bottleneck while protecting correctness and downstream guardrails Stable 2.0 Enterprise Operate AI capabilities with enforceable governance across tenants, jurisdictions, and risk tiers Stable 2.0 Release Promote a signed artifact through progressive exposure with objective abort criteria Stable 2.0 Hotfix Contain an active production defect with the smallest reversible intervention Stable 2.0 Root Cause Explain why an incident occurred and prioritize controls that prevent or limit recurrence Stable 2.0 Completeness contract Each pattern contains README, problem, context, workflow, prompt, agent, subagents, skills, hooks, checklist, concrete example, failures, and enterprise notes. Run node validate-pattern-library.mjs after edits; it verifies structure, local links, placeholders, prompt/agent controls, exact duplicate prose, and pairwise corpus similarity. Selection rule Select from the documented trigger, then execute that pattern's domain workflow. Effect approval is necessary but never substitutes for domain evidence, method, verification, or recovery. Tradeoffs Maintaining distinct methods costs more than a shared template. That cost is required because planning, debugging, migration, incident analysis, and the other domains fail in materially different ways. Anti-patterns Do not satisfy the library by renaming nouns in generic prose. Repeated substantive lines or high pairwise similarity fail validation. Enterprise considerations Organizations map the pattern-specific artifacts to their control catalog, identity system, evidence retention, jurisdiction, incident process, and separation-of-duties model. Checklist - [ ] Twelve indexed patterns each contain thirteen components - [ ] Domain workflows, roles, skills, hooks, failures, examples, citations, and enterprise controls are distinct - [ ] Similarity and integrity validation passes Changelog - 2026-07-16: Replaced generic scaffolding with domain-specific production guidance.

docs.text: Root Cause: Enterprise Operations Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose Scale root cause practice across regulated and multi-team environments without weakening its domain controls. Tailored controls Legal review protects privilege without deleting operational truth. HR policy separates accountability from blame; interview access is controlled, labor rules respected, and personal data minimized. Systemic action trends are reported across business units. Governance model Name an accountable service owner, evidence owners, effect approvers, and an independent control assessor. Version the pattern, policy, model, tools, and artifacts as one audit record. For the Root Cause enterprise notes contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Metrics and assurance - Control dashboard reports 100% causal edges cite evidence. - Control dashboard reports timeline uncertainty is explicit. - Control dashboard reports actions favor engineered controls over reminders. - Control dashboard reports effectiveness reviewed at 30/60/90 days. Sample completed records quarterly and after a material incident. Test both control design and operating effectiveness; a documented control that did not run is a failure. For the Root Cause enterprise notes contract, gate 2 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Tradeoffs Central governance improves consistency but can bottleneck specialist work; publish versioned paved roads and time-bound exceptions instead of local bypasses. For the Root Cause enterprise notes contract, gate 3 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Anti-patterns Vendor certification does not assure the deployed workflow, and indefinite raw-prompt retention increases rather than reduces risk. docs.text: Root Cause: Worked Production Example Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Scenario and artifacts INC-447 delayed payroll for 18,204 employees. Timeline TL-447 reconciles NTP offsets across deploy d-993, queue q-payroll, and alert a-81. Graph CG-447 shows malformed tenant config plus non-idempotent retry and a disabled saturation alert; replay CF-12 proves removing either retry defect or config bypass prevents impact. Actions eliminate bypass, enforce idempotency, isolate tenant queues, and restore alert coverage. Execution 1. Set a blameless charter: explain system conditions, not individual fault; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 2. Reconstruct a UTC timeline from independent sources and mark uncertainty; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 3. Build a causal graph from initiating event through mechanisms to impact; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 4. Distinguish root mechanisms, contributing conditions, and latent controls; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 5. Test each causal edge against evidence and alternative explanations; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 6. Use five-whys only as an interview prompt; branch the graph when causes diverge; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 7. Run counterfactual tests: remove each condition and predict whether impact persists; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 8. Prioritize actions: eliminate hazard, add prevention, reduce blast radius, improve detection, then procedure/training; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 9. Assign owners, dates, leading indicators, and effectiveness review; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. 10. Publish factual narrative; revisit after actions demonstrate sustained effectiveness; the record attaches the resulting artifact to the example's primary change or incident ID. Verification - The owner records raw evidence that 100% causal edges cite evidence. - The owner records raw evidence that timeline uncertainty is explicit. - The owner records raw evidence that actions favor engineered controls over reminders. - The owner records raw evidence that effectiveness reviewed at 30/60/90 days. Rollback exercise The team demonstrates it can withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. The exercise records elapsed time, restored revision, data reconciliation where applicable, and residual exposure. Tradeoffs This example favors bounded exposure and inspectable evidence over fastest possible completion. For the Root Cause examples example contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Anti-patterns The concrete identifiers are local example artifacts, not phantom web links; replacing them with unresolved markers or invented results, or verbal approval invalidates the example. For the Root Cause examples example contract, gate 2 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Enterprise considerations The evidence package records identities, policy revisions, source/artifact hashes, approvals, classification, retention, and any exception expiry. For the Root Cause examples example contract, gate 3 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Checklist - [ ] Every stated artifact has an owner and storage location in the system of record - [ ] Reported outcomes come from executed checks Changelog - 2026-07-16: Replaced generic scaffolding with domain-specific production guidance.

docs.text: Root Cause: Problem Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose The Root Cause pattern exists because teams need to explain why an incident occurred and prioritize controls that prevent or limit recurrence, yet commonly act before the domain evidence can support that outcome. Observable problem 1. When a material incident is stabilized, an undocumented assumption can become a production decision. 2. When a near miss reveals systemic exposure, an undocumented assumption can become a production decision. 3. When the same failure class recurs, an undocumented assumption can become a production decision. Quality boundary The pattern is complete only when 100% causal edges cite evidence; timeline uncertainty is explicit; actions favor engineered controls over reminders; effectiveness reviewed at 30/60/90 days. Its scope excludes routine work that cannot trigger the stated failure modes. Tradeoffs A stricter entry test may defer work with weak evidence; proceeding would transfer unknown risk to operators and users. For the Root Cause problem contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Anti-patterns Do not rewrite a requested solution as the problem statement. State the violated invariant, affected population, baseline, target, and non-goals. For the Root Cause problem contract, gate 2 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Enterprise considerations The accountable service owner accepts the problem statement; risk or compliance owners accept any material residual exposure. For the Root Cause problem contract, gate 3 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Checklist - [ ] Trigger and affected population are quantified - [ ] Baseline and desired outcome are distinguishable - [ ] Scope and non-goals have named owners Changelog - 2026-07-16: Replaced generic scaffolding with domain-specific production guidance.

For the Root Cause prompt contract, gate 4 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. For the Root Cause prompt contract, gate 5 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Applicability - a material incident is stabilized - a near miss reveals systemic exposure - the same failure class recurs Evidence - normalized incident timeline - logs, traces, metrics, and deploys - decision and communication records - architecture and control design - interviews and counterfactual experiments Components Problem · Context · Workflow · Prompt · Agent · Subagents · Skills · Hooks · Checklist · Example · Failures · Enterprise README is component thirteen. Outcome measures - 100% causal edges cite evidence - timeline uncertainty is explicit - actions favor engineered controls over reminders - effectiveness reviewed at 30/60/90 days Rollback Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Tradeoffs Applying Root Cause discipline spends review and evidence time before closure; use it only when one of its triggers is present. Anti-patterns Skipping its domain workflow while retaining the label creates false assurance. Evidence and measured outcomes, not document completion, determine success. For the Root Cause README contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. docs.title: Root Cause: Skills
docs.description: Define the procedures unique to competent root cause work.
docs.text: Root Cause: Skills Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose Define the procedures unique to competent root cause work. Timeline reconstruction Trigger: Workflow step 1 needs timeline reconstruction. Procedure: merge sources with clock offsets and confidence; record inputs, transformations, and decision thresholds. Verification: an independent practitioner reproduces the artifact from cited sources. Unhappy path: stop the dependent workflow step and request the missing authority or evidence. Causal graphing Trigger: Workflow step 2 needs causal graphing. Procedure: represent necessary, sufficient, and contributing conditions; record inputs, transformations, and decision thresholds. Verification: an independent practitioner reproduces the artifact from cited sources. Unhappy path: stop the dependent workflow step and request the missing authority or evidence. Counterfactual testing Trigger: Workflow step 3 needs counterfactual testing. Procedure: predict and test outcomes with conditions removed; record inputs, transformations, and decision thresholds. Verification: an independent practitioner reproduces the artifact from cited sources. Unhappy path: stop the dependent workflow step and request the missing authority or evidence. Corrective-action hierarchy Trigger: Workflow step 4 needs corrective-action hierarchy. Procedure: prefer elimination and engineered prevention over training; record inputs, transformations, and decision thresholds. Verification: an independent practitioner reproduces the artifact from cited sources. Unhappy path: stop the dependent workflow step and request the missing authority or evidence. Tradeoffs Skill verification costs a second pass; it prevents polished but non-reproducible analysis. For the Root Cause skills contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Anti-patterns A skill name without trigger, procedure, output, and unhappy path is not an operational skill. For the Root Cause skills contract, gate 2 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Enterprise considerations Version each skill, assign an owner, and review it after incidents, policy changes, or tool upgrades. For the Root Cause skills contract, gate 3 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Checklist - [ ] timeline reconstruction produced a reproducible artifact - [ ] causal graphing produced a reproducible artifact - [ ] counterfactual testing produced a reproducible artifact - [ ] corrective-action hierarchy produced a reproducible artifact Changelog - 2026-07-16: Replaced generic scaffolding with domain-specific production guidance.

docs.title: Root Cause: Workflow
docs.description: Execute the domain method for explain why an incident occurred and prioritize controls that prevent or limit recurrence.
docs.text: Root Cause: Workflow Version: 2.0 Updated: 2026-07-16 Status: Stable Purpose Execute the domain method for explain why an incident occurred and prioritize controls that prevent or limit recurrence. Procedure 1. Set a blameless. Set a blameless charter: explain system conditions, not individual fault. 2. Reconstruct a UTC. Reconstruct a UTC timeline from independent sources and mark uncertainty. 3. Build a causal. Build a causal graph from initiating event through mechanisms to impact. 4. Distinguish root mechanisms,. Distinguish root mechanisms, contributing conditions, and latent controls. 5. Test each causal. Test each causal edge against evidence and alternative explanations. 6. Use five-whys only. Use five-whys only as an interview prompt; branch the graph when causes diverge. 7. Run counterfactual tests:. Run counterfactual tests: remove each condition and predict whether impact persists. 8. Prioritize actions: eliminate. Prioritize actions: eliminate hazard, add prevention, reduce blast radius, improve detection, then procedure/training. 9. Assign owners, dates,. Assign owners, dates, leading indicators, and effectiveness review. 10. Publish factual narrative;. Publish factual narrative; revisit after actions demonstrate sustained effectiveness. Verification - 100% causal edges cite evidence - timeline uncertainty is explicit - actions favor engineered controls over reminders - effectiveness reviewed at 30/60/90 days Tradeoffs The ordered workflow limits parallelism where later conclusions depend on earlier evidence; independent collection may run concurrently. For the Root Cause workflow contract, gate 1 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Anti-patterns A generic intake/approval loop is not this workflow. Each numbered domain operation produces an inspectable artifact. For the Root Cause workflow contract, gate 2 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Enterprise considerations Approvals attach to resulting effects, while evidence gathering remains read-only and least-privileged. For the Root Cause workflow contract, gate 3 is evidenced by "100% causal edges cite evidence"; failure invokes this domain recovery: Withdraw unsupported causal claims, preserve the draft, and reopen timeline or experiment collection. Checklist - [ ] Set a blameless charter: explain system conditions, not individual fault - [ ] Reconstruct a UTC timeline from independent sources and mark uncertainty - [ ] Build a causal graph from initiating event through mechanisms to impact - [ ] Distinguish root mechanisms, contributing conditions, and latent controls - [ ] Test each causal edge against evidence and alternative explanations - [ ] Use five-whys only as an interview prompt; branch the graph when causes diverge - [ ] Run counterfactual tests: remove each condition and predict whether impact persists - [ ] Prioritize actions: eliminate hazard, add prevention, reduce blast radius, improve detection, then procedure/training - [ ] Assign owners, dates, leading indicators, and effectiveness review - [ ] Publish factual narrative; revisit after actions demonstrate sustained effectiveness Changelog - 2026-07-16: Replaced generic scaffolding with domain-specific production guidance.

docs.title: Open AI Engineering Standard (OAIES)
docs.description: License: MIT
docs.text: Open AI Engineering Standard (OAIES) The definitive open-source standard for building production-grade AI systems. Not a tutorial. Not a template. A standard — opinionated, battle-tested, and built by engineers who ship. License: MIT Version Standard --- Why This Exists Every serious engineering discipline has a standard. - Web: React, Next.js conventions - APIs: REST, OpenAPI, GraphQL - DevOps: The Twelve-Factor App - AI Engineering: Nothing. Until now. Most AI repositories give you "here are five ways to do X." This repository gives you one way — the right way — informed by production deployments, enterprise constraints, and the collective wisdom of engineers who have shipped AI systems at scale. If you are starting any AI product, you fork this first. --- Maturity Model This repository is structured as a 10-level AI Engineering Maturity Model. Enter at your current level. Ascend deliberately. Level Name When You're Ready ------- ------ ------------------- L0 AI Foundations You're new to building with LLMs L1 Prompt Engineering You understand tokens and context L2 Context Engineering You're building multi-turn systems L3 Skill Engineering You're automating recurring workflows L4 Agent Engineering You're building autonomous agents L5 Multi-Agent Systems You're orchestrating agent networks L6 Memory & Knowledge You need persistent agent memory L7 LLMOps You're running AI in production L8 AI SDLC You're building AI-first processes L9 Enterprise AI You need governance and compliance L10 AI Org Playbook You're building an AI-first organization --- The Standard Workflow Every feature. Every time. No exceptions. See the AI SDLC for the complete workflow specification with prompts for every stage. --- What's Inside 🏗️ Core Sections (Maturity Levels) - 00-foundations/ — How LLMs think, the harness principle, failure modes - 01-prompt-engineering/ — XML-structured prompts, patterns, anti-patterns - 02-context-engineering/ — Context fidelity, progressive disclosure, state management - 03-skill-engineering/ — 26 reusable agent skills - 04-agent-engineering/ — 20 agent definitions, subagents, hooks - 05-multi-agent-systems/ — Orchestration patterns, A2A communication - 06-memory-knowledge/ — Memory types, knowledge graphs, hybrid RAG - 07-llmops/ — Evaluation, PromptOps, cost optimization, observability - 08-ai-sdlc/ — Complete SDLC with 15 production prompts - 09-enterprise-ai/ — Governance, security, compliance, templates - 10-ai-org-playbook/ — Roles, operating models, culture ⭐ Unique Differentiators - patterns/ — 12 AI Engineering Patterns (full 13-component specification — nobody else has this) - cookbook/ — AI Cookbook for 18 technology stacks - mcps/ — 24 production-ready MCP integration specs 🛠️ Operational Resources - prompts/ — Standard prompt library (cross-referenced with SDLC) - skills/ — All 26 skills (installable in .claude/skills/) - agents/ — All 20 agent definitions (installable in .claude/agents/) - hooks/ — 12 lifecycle hooks (pre/post code, commit, review, deploy) - checklists/ — Quality gates for every stage - evaluation/ — RAGAS, DeepEval, Promptfoo setup guides - security/ — Prompt injection defense, sandboxing, red teaming - observability/ — OpenTelemetry, LangSmith, Langfuse, dashboards - templates/ — ADR, PRD, RFC, Runbook, Playbook templates - papers/ — Curated breakthrough research papers - resources/ — Books, talks, repositories, standards --- Quick Start Use with Claude Code Use with Cursor / Windsurf / Roo Use standalone Browse the maturity model from Level 0 and follow the standard workflow defined in Level 8. --- Design Principles Principle What It Means ----------- --------------- Opinionated One standard, not a menu of options Production-first Every recommendation is battle-tested Enterprise-ready Governance, compliance, and audit trails built in Living standard Updated quarterly with technology radar insights Context-complete Every decision includes Why, When, Tradeoffs, Anti-patterns --- The 50/50 Rule 50% AI reasoning. 50% deterministic code. The biggest mistake in AI engineering is treating the LLM as the entire system. The model is one component. The deterministic harness around it — validation, authorization, execution, logging — is equally important. This repository enforces both halves equally. --- Contributing Read CONTRIBUTING.md before opening a PR. The standard for contributions is high by design. Every addition must include: - Clear "Why" rationale - Documented tradeoffs - At least one anti-pattern - Enterprise consideration - Working example --- Versioning Version Focus --------- ------- v1.0 AI Foundations, Prompt Engineering, Context Engineering v2.0 Agent Engineering, Multi-Agent Systems v3.0 LLMOps, AI SDLC v4.0 Enterprise AI, AI Org Playbook v5.0 Patterns Library complete v10.0 Full Cookbook across all technology stacks --- License MIT — Use it, adapt it, build on it. If it helps you, give it a star and consider contributing back. --- OAIES v1.0 — "The standard doesn't tell you what you can do. It tells you what you must do."

docs.title: OAIES Kernel and Applicability
docs.description: Define the boundary, language, identifiers, classifications, and applicability rules used by every OAIES conformance claim.
docs.text: OAIES Kernel and Applicability Version: 1.0.0 Published: 2026-07-16 Status: Normative Purpose Define the boundary, language, identifiers, classifications, and applicability rules used by every OAIES conformance claim. Why An assessor cannot test controls consistently when system boundaries, requirement words, or risk classifications are implicit. A fixed classification method prevents teams from reducing obligations by renaming a workload or excluding risky dependencies. How 1. Scope The kernel applies to an AI system used in production or to make decisions that affect real people, assets, rights, safety, security, or business operations. The assessed system includes models, prompts, retrieval sources, memory, tools, orchestrators, deterministic safeguards, user interfaces, operators, deployment infrastructure, telemetry, and third-party services that can affect output or action. Research prototypes are outside scope only while isolated from production data, users, decisions, and side effects. A prototype becomes in scope when any of those conditions ceases to hold. 2. Terminology Term Normative meaning --- --- AI system Sociotechnical system that uses an AI model to produce predictions, content, recommendations, decisions, or actions. System boundary Components, people, data, interfaces, dependencies, environments, and processes included in a claim. Control Uniquely identified, testable normative requirement. Objective evidence Verifiable record demonstrating design, implementation, or operation for a stated period and scope. Workload profile Functional pattern that determines profile-specific controls. Autonomy level Maximum authority to select or execute consequential actions without synchronous human approval. Impact level Severity of reasonably foreseeable harm from intended use, misuse, or failure. High-impact system System classified I3 under this standard or designated high-risk/high-impact by applicable law or policy. System owner Named person accountable for lifecycle risk and the conformance claim. Control owner Named person accountable for operating a control and maintaining evidence. SoA Statement of Applicability: authoritative control inventory and disposition for one assessed system. Exception Time-bound approval to leave an applicable control partly or wholly unsatisfied. Compensating control Alternative safeguard that reduces the same risk to an accepted residual level. Assessment period Time interval for which operating effectiveness is evaluated. Material change Change capable of altering profile, autonomy, impact, control design, or residual risk. These terms align with the system-oriented risk vocabulary of NIST AI RMF 1.0 and the management-system approach of ISO/IEC 42001:2023. 3. Requirement Language The uppercase requirement vocabulary is interpreted exactly as described by RFC 2119 and RFC 8174. Keyword OAIES interpretation --- --- MUST / MUST NOT Absolute requirement or prohibition. Non-implementation is a nonconformity unless an allowed exception is active. SHOULD / SHOULD NOT Strong recommendation. Departure requires recorded rationale in the SoA but is not itself a nonconformity. MAY Permitted option that creates no conformance obligation unless selected by another control. Only statements with a control ID create OAIES requirements. Normative tables pair each uppercase requirement with objective evidence. 4. Control Identifiers Control IDs are immutable and use the pattern OAIES-DOMAIN-NNN, where DOMAIN is a registered three-letter code and NNN is a zero-padded sequence. Domain Code Subject --- --- --- Governance GOV ownership, boundary, classification, applicability Risk RSK risk analysis, acceptance, high-impact oversight Data DAT data, retrieval, provenance, privacy Model MOD model selection, evaluation, change Agent AGT tools, autonomy, actions, memory Security SEC abuse, access, isolation, supply chain Operations OPS release, observability, incident response Assurance ASR evidence, assessment, conformance An identifier is never reused. Retired IDs remain reserved. Subrequirements append a lowercase letter only when independently testable, such as OAIES-AGT-004a. 5. Workload Profiles Select every profile describing production behavior; profiles are cumulative. Code Profile Inclusion test Primary added risk --- --- --- --- P1 Assistant Generates content or advice without executing external side effects misleading, unsafe, or sensitive output P2 RAG Uses retrieved sources at inference time poisoned, unauthorized, stale, or ungrounded context P3 Coding agent Reads, writes, reviews, or executes software artifacts vulnerable code, secret exposure, destructive execution P4 Transactional agent Initiates or changes external records, payments, messages, permissions, or physical state unauthorized or irreversible action P5 Multi-agent Delegates among two or more model-driven agents authority propagation, coordination failure, opaque provenance P6 High-impact Meets I3 or a legal/policy high-impact designation harm to rights, safety, essential access, or livelihood 6. Autonomy and Impact Classify the maximum deployed capability, not intended average behavior. Level Autonomy definition Required governance posture --- --- --- A0 No action; output is not used for a consequential decision standard review A1 Recommends; a human independently decides and executes meaningful human review A2 Executes reversible, bounded actions with pre-authorization least privilege, action logs, tested rollback A3 Executes consequential or externally visible actions without per-action approval independent assurance, runtime policy enforcement, emergency stop A4 Pursues open-ended goals or can alter its own authority, tools, or safeguards prohibited unless an approved high-impact governance program explicitly authorizes a bounded deployment Level Impact definition Examples --- --- --- I0 Negligible; no credible harm beyond inconvenience internal drafting with no sensitive data I1 Limited, recoverable harm low-value support error, reversible workflow delay I2 Material financial, security, privacy, operational, or reputational harm production code change, customer transaction, sensitive-data disclosure I3 Severe or systemic harm to safety, rights, livelihood, essential services, or many affected persons employment, credit, healthcare, critical infrastructure, biometric categorization If evidence supports multiple levels, select the highest. Legal designation overrides a lower internal classification. The EU AI Act is authoritative for EU prohibited and high-risk classifications; OAIES does not replace legal analysis. 7. Applicability Algorithm 1. Establish intended use, reasonably foreseeable misuse, affected parties, data, environments, dependencies, and side effects. 2. Select all workload profiles. 3. Assign autonomy and impact levels using maximum credible deployed capability. 4. Apply universal controls, all selected profile controls, and all autonomy/impact overlays. 5. Add legal, contractual, and organization-specific controls. 6. Record each control as applicable, not applicable, or applicable with exception in the SoA. 7. Obtain approvals and reassess on every material change. 8. Kernel Controls Control ID Normative requirement Applicability Objective evidence --- --- --- --- OAIES-GOV-001 The organization MUST maintain an approved system boundary covering every component and dependency capable of affecting outputs or actions. Universal Versioned boundary record, architecture/data-flow diagram, dependency inventory, owner approval OAIES-GOV-002 The organization MUST name one system owner and a control owner for every applicable control. Universal Signed ownership register and SoA owner fields OAIES-GOV-003 The system owner MUST classify all applicable workload profiles, autonomy level, and impact level before production use and after material change. Universal Dated classification record with rationale, approver, and change history OAIES-GOV-004 The SoA MUST include every control in the claimed OAIES version and record its applicability disposition and rationale. Universal Complete version-controlled SoA; automated or manual completeness reconciliation OAIES-GOV-005 A not-applicable disposition MUST NOT be used solely because implementation is costly, difficult, outsourced, or incomplete. Universal SoA rationales tied to boundary facts; assessor challenge log OAIES-GOV-006 Third-party components MUST remain inside the system boundary wherever their behavior can affect conformance. Universal Supplier inventory, contracts/assurance reports, boundary diagram, shared-responsibility matrix OAIES-RSK-001 A4 deployment MUST NOT enter production without documented executive authorization, independent risk assessment, bounded authority, and tested containment. A4 Signed authorization, independent assessment report, authority policy, containment test results Tradeoffs Decision Benefit Cost --- --- --- Cumulative profiles Prevents under-scoping hybrid systems More controls apply Highest-capability classification Covers rare but severe behavior Can overstate routine operating risk Immutable IDs Stable evidence and mappings Corrections require new IDs or revisions Third parties in boundary Preserves accountability Supplier evidence may be difficult to obtain Anti-patterns - Profile shopping: selecting only the least demanding profile for a hybrid workload. - Boundary laundering: excluding a model provider, vector store, plugin, or human operation because it is outsourced. - Average-case autonomy: labeling an agent A1 because humans usually review, although production permissions permit autonomous execution. - Control-ID recycling: assigning retired identifiers to unrelated requirements and invalidating historical mappings. Enterprise Considerations Use a central system inventory as the source of truth for owners, classifications, SoAs, exceptions, and claims. Integrate material-change triggers with architecture review, procurement, model registry, data governance, identity governance, and release management. Record jurisdiction-specific classifications separately; do not collapse legal status into OAIES impact alone. Checklist - [ ] Boundary includes models, data, tools, people, infrastructure, and suppliers. - [ ] All six workload inclusion tests were evaluated. - [ ] Autonomy reflects maximum production authority. - [ ] Impact reflects foreseeable misuse and failure. - [ ] All controls in the claimed version appear in the SoA. - [ ] Owners and approvals are current. - [ ] Material-change triggers are integrated into release governance. Authoritative References - RFC 2119 — Key words for use in RFCs - RFC 8174 — Ambiguity of uppercase and lowercase key words - NIST AI RMF 1.0 - NIST AI 600-1 — Generative AI Profile - ISO/IEC 42001:2023 - Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Changelog Version Date Change --- --- --- 1.0.0 2026-07-16 Defined scope, vocabulary, requirement language, IDs, profiles, risk levels, and applicability.

docs.title: OAIES Normative Controls
docs.description: Define the minimum control baseline for OAIES-conformant AI systems. Each requirement is testable and names the objective evidence expected by an assessor.
docs.text: OAIES Normative Controls Version: 1.0.1 Published: 2026-07-16 Status: Normative Purpose Define the minimum control baseline for OAIES-conformant AI systems. Each requirement is testable and names the objective evidence expected by an assessor. Why AI assurance fails when controls describe aspirations instead of observable safeguards. This catalog binds each obligation to applicability and evidence so design adequacy and operating effectiveness can be assessed separately. How Apply universal controls first, then every selected workload, autonomy, and impact overlay. Evidence examples are minimum evidence classes, not exhaustive implementation prescriptions. Equivalent evidence is acceptable when it is authentic, scoped, attributable, timely, and reproducible. Universal Governance and Risk Controls Control ID Normative requirement Applicability Objective evidence --- --- --- --- OAIES-RSK-002 The system owner MUST maintain a risk register covering intended use, foreseeable misuse, affected parties, failure modes, likelihood, impact, safeguards, residual risk, and treatment owner. Universal Approved risk register linked to system version and review history OAIES-RSK-003 Residual risks above the organization’s approved tolerance MUST NOT be accepted by the system owner alone. Universal Risk policy, approval matrix, signed acceptance by authorized risk owner OAIES-MOD-001 The organization MUST define measurable acceptance criteria and evaluate the complete system against representative and adversarial cases before release. Universal Versioned evaluation plan, dataset lineage, executable results, threshold decision OAIES-MOD-002 Production model, prompt, policy, tool, and configuration versions MUST be uniquely identifiable and reproducible. Universal Immutable release manifest, hashes/versions, configuration snapshot, rebuild or replay result OAIES-MOD-003 Material model or prompt changes MUST NOT bypass regression, safety, and security gates. Universal Change diff, CI/release gate logs, evaluation comparison, approval record OAIES-DAT-001 Data used for training, tuning, retrieval, evaluation, or inference MUST have documented provenance, permitted purpose, sensitivity, retention, and responsible owner. Universal Data inventory, lineage records, legal basis/license, classification and retention policy OAIES-DAT-002 Sensitive data MUST be minimized and protected in prompts, logs, memory, evaluation sets, and outputs according to its classification. Where sensitive data is processed Data-flow map, minimization decision, access controls, encryption settings, DLP test results OAIES-SEC-001 Identity and access controls MUST enforce least privilege for models, tools, data stores, administrative interfaces, and service accounts. Universal Access matrix, policy configuration, entitlement review, denied-access tests OAIES-SEC-002 Untrusted input and model output MUST be treated as data rather than executable authority across trust boundaries. Universal Threat model, parser/validator policy, sandbox configuration, injection test results OAIES-SEC-003 Secrets MUST NOT be embedded in prompts, source artifacts, model context, logs, or generated output. Universal Secret-scanning results, vault references, redacted telemetry sample, incident review OAIES-OPS-001 Production releases MUST use an approved, attributable, reversible change process with separation appropriate to impact. Universal Release ticket, approver identity, deployment log, rollback plan and exercise OAIES-OPS-002 The organization MUST monitor safety, security, quality, availability, cost, and policy-relevant events at frequencies justified by risk.
